title: The solar system: planets, their satellites, and the true distances between them

summary.text: Ganymede, a moon of Jupiter, is wider than the planet Mercury. So what makes a world a planet and not a moon? In this lesson you will balance heavy and light dough balls to find the point they go round, and set a marble Earth and a peppercorn Moon at the true distance.
summary.art: A kitchen table with a pencil balanced on a child's finger, a big dough ball on one end and a small one on the other, and beside it a marble and a peppercorn 48 centimetres apart along a ruler.

intro.hook: Ganymede is a moon of Jupiter, and it is wider than the planet Mercury. Pluto was a planet when your grandparents went to school, and today it is not. If size is not the test, what makes one world a planet and another a satellite?
intro.text: In this lesson you find the answer, and you test it with your own hands. First you set a marble Earth and a peppercorn Moon the right distance apart. Then you balance two dough balls on a pencil, to find the point that two worlds both go round. You also find out how much more dough a ball needs when it is twice as wide. At the end you can say why Pluto's name changed, and where the solar system ends.
intro.art: Mercury and Ganymede drawn side by side at the same scale, Ganymede slightly the wider of the two, with Jupiter's curved edge filling the background behind Ganymede.

outcomes: By the end I can name the eight planets in order, and say what sets the Earth apart.
By the end I can tell a star, planet, dwarf planet and satellite apart by what each goes round. I can say that the Pole Star is a star far outside the solar system, and that it shows north.
By the end I can explain why a satellite can be bigger than a planet, using Ganymede and Mercury.
By the end I can use the balance rule to find the point that two worlds both go round.
By the end I can build a true model of the Earth, the Moon and the Sun on one scale.
By the end I can explain why a ball twice as wide holds eight times as much.
By the end I can give the three tests for a planet, and one argument on each side about Pluto.
By the end I can give three different answers to where the solar system ends.

terms.meaning: The Sun and everything that goes round it: eight planets, their moons, dwarf planets, asteroids, comets and dust. Gravity holds it all together.
terms.example: The Earth, the Moon, Jupiter, Pluto and Halley's Comet all belong to the solar system.
terms.art: The Sun with eight planets on their paths, a belt of small rocks between Mars and Jupiter, and a comet with a tail.

terms.meaning: A huge ball of very hot gas that makes its own light and heat. The Sun is the star nearest to us.
terms.example: The Sun is a star. Every other star in the night sky is a far-away sun.
terms.art: The Sun drawn as a glowing ball, with a few tiny far stars in a dark sky behind it.

terms.meaning: A large round world that goes round a star and gives off no light of its own. A planet has also cleared its path, which means that no other large bodies share the path it travels round the Sun.
terms.example: The Earth is a planet. It goes round the Sun once in about 365 days.
terms.art: The Earth on its path round the Sun, half lit by sunlight and half dark.

terms.meaning: The path one body follows round another body. Gravity keeps the body on that path.
terms.example: The Moon's orbit round the Earth takes about 27 days. The Earth's orbit round the Sun takes one year.
terms.art: A dotted oval path round the Earth with the Moon on it and an arrow showing the direction.

terms.meaning: A body that goes round a planet or another world that is not a star. A natural satellite is also called a moon.
terms.example: The Moon is the Earth's natural satellite. Ganymede is a satellite of Jupiter.
terms.art: Jupiter with four moons on their paths round it, one of them labelled Ganymede.

terms.meaning: A machine that people have put into orbit. It goes round the Earth or another world, as a moon does.
terms.example: The International Space Station goes round the Earth about 400 kilometres up. India's first satellite was Aryabhata, in 1975.
terms.art: A satellite with two flat solar panels passing above the outline of India.

terms.meaning: A round world that goes round the Sun but has not cleared other bodies from its path. It is not a satellite of anything.
terms.example: Pluto, Ceres and Eris are dwarf planets. Pluto shares its path with thousands of icy bodies.
terms.art: Small round Pluto among many small icy lumps spread along the same wide path.

terms.meaning: A rocky or metal body that goes round the Sun and is too small to pull itself round. Most asteroids are between Mars and Jupiter.
terms.example: Vesta is an asteroid about 525 kilometres wide. Most asteroids are far smaller and shaped like lumpy potatoes.
terms.art: A grey lumpy rock shaped like a potato, covered in small craters, floating in dark space.

terms.meaning: A wide ring of icy bodies beyond Neptune. It lies about 30 to 50 times as far from the Sun as the Earth does.
terms.example: Pluto is one of the largest bodies in the Kuiper belt. You say the name 'KY-per'.
terms.art: The eight planets' paths seen from above, with a broad hazy ring of small icy dots outside Neptune's path.

terms.meaning: The point between two bodies where they would balance, as on a see-saw. Two worlds held by gravity both go round this point. Scientists call it the barycentre.
terms.example: The balance point of the Earth and the Moon is inside the Earth, about 4,700 kilometres from its centre.
terms.art: The Earth cut open to show a small cross inside it, well away from the centre, on the side facing the Moon.

terms.meaning: How much matter a thing is made of. Mass is measured in kilograms. A body with more mass has a stronger pull of gravity.
terms.example: The Earth has 81 times the mass of the Moon. The Sun has about 333,000 times the mass of the Earth.
terms.art: A balance with one large ball in one pan and 81 small balls heaped in the other pan, level.

terms.meaning: The width of a ball or a circle, measured straight through its centre.
terms.example: The Earth's diameter is about 12,742 kilometres. The Moon's is about 3,474 kilometres.
terms.art: A ball cut in half with a ruler line drawn straight across through the centre.

terms.meaning: How much space a thing takes up. A ball twice as wide has eight times the volume.
terms.example: Jupiter is about 11 times as wide as the Earth. Its volume is about 1,300 times the Earth's.
terms.art: One small dough ball beside a ball twice as wide, with eight small balls lined up under the big one.

terms.meaning: The rule that turns real sizes into model sizes. One scale must be used for every size and every distance in a true model.
terms.example: On the scale of 1 centimetre to 8,000 kilometres, the Earth is a marble. The Moon is a peppercorn 48 centimetres away.
terms.art: A marble and a peppercorn on a table with a ruler between them, and a label saying 1 cm = 8,000 km.

terms.meaning: The distance from the Earth to the Sun, about 150 million kilometres. It is used to measure the solar system. The short form is AU.
terms.example: Jupiter is about 5 astronomical units from the Sun. Neptune is about 30.
terms.art: A long line from the Sun to Neptune marked in 30 equal steps, with the Earth at step 1.

terms.meaning: One full trip of a body round another body. One revolution of the Earth round the Sun is one year.
terms.example: Mercury makes one revolution in 88 days. Neptune takes about 165 years.
terms.art: The Earth shown at four places on its path round the Sun, with an arrow going all the way round.

terms.meaning: The huge bubble of thin gas that the Sun blows out around itself. Its edge is far beyond all the planets.
terms.example: The spacecraft Voyager 1 left the heliosphere in 2012, about 120 times as far from the Sun as the Earth.
terms.art: The Sun and planets as a tiny dot inside a large, soft-edged bubble, with a small spacecraft just outside the bubble.

terms.meaning: The imaginary line through a spinning world, from one pole to the other. The Earth spins on its axis once in about 24 hours.
terms.example: The Earth's axis leans about 23.5 degrees. Uranus leans so far that it spins almost on its side.
terms.art: The Earth with a straight line through it from the North Pole to the South Pole, leaning a little to one side, and a curved arrow showing the spin.

terms.meaning: A star that sits almost exactly above the Earth's north pole, so it hardly seems to move as the night goes on. It is far outside the solar system.
terms.example: On a clear night, travellers face the Pole Star to find north.
terms.art: The night sky over a rooftop, with curved trails of stars circling round one bright star that stays still.

explanations.concept: Star, planet or satellite: what a body goes round decides the name
explanations.definition: A star makes its own light. A planet is a large round world that goes round a star. A satellite goes round a planet or another world that is not a star.
explanations.description: The Sun is a star, because it makes light and heat deep inside itself. The Earth makes no light, and it goes round the Sun, so it is a planet. The Moon goes round the Earth, so it is a satellite. These names say nothing about size. Ganymede is 5,268 kilometres wide and Mercury is 4,879 kilometres wide. Ganymede is the wider world, yet it is a satellite, because it goes round Jupiter. If Ganymede went round the Sun alone, it would be called a planet.
examples: The Sun makes its own light, so it is a star.
Mercury goes round the Sun, so it is a planet, even though it is smaller than two moons.
Ganymede and Titan are both wider than Mercury. But they go round Jupiter and Saturn, so they are satellites.
explanations.art: Three small pictures in a row: the Sun glowing, the Earth on a path round the Sun, and the Moon on a path round the Earth, each with an arrow showing what it goes round.

explanations.concept: The eight planets, and the Earth among them
explanations.definition: Eight planets go round the Sun. In order from the Sun they are Mercury, Venus, the Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.
explanations.description: The first four are small and made of rock and metal. The next four are giants made mostly of gas and ice. The Earth is the third planet and the largest of the four rocky ones. It is the only planet with seas of liquid water on its surface. It is the only world where we know living beings exist. Its air is about one-fifth oxygen, and living beings made nearly all of that oxygen. The Earth also has one very large Moon. All eight planets go round the Sun the same way, on paths that lie almost flat, like rings on a plate.
examples: Widths in kilometres: Mercury 4,879, Venus 12,104, the Earth 12,742, Mars 6,779.
Widths in kilometres: Jupiter 139,820, Saturn 116,460, Uranus 50,724, Neptune 49,244.
Distance from the Sun in astronomical units: Mercury 0.4, Venus 0.7, the Earth 1, Mars 1.5, Jupiter 5.2, Saturn 9.5, Uranus 19, Neptune 30.
explanations.art: The eight planets in a row in order from the Sun, drawn at the right sizes compared with each other, with the Earth marked by a small arrow.

explanations.concept: Satellites: natural ones and the ones people make
explanations.definition: A natural satellite, or moon, is a body that goes round a planet without anyone putting it there. An artificial satellite is a machine that people have put into orbit.
explanations.description: Mercury and Venus have no moons. The Earth has one and Mars has two. The giant planets have many. By 2025, astronomers had counted about 95 moons for Jupiter and more than 270 for Saturn. They had counted about 28 for Uranus and 16 for Neptune. The counts keep rising. Seven moons are wider than Pluto, and our Moon is one of them. People have also made satellites since 1957. The International Space Station goes round the Earth about 400 kilometres up, once every 90 minutes. Television and weather satellites sit about 36,000 kilometres up. A spacecraft that goes round the Moon or Mars is a satellite of that world.
examples: Natural satellites: the Moon, Ganymede, Titan, and Phobos, a moon of Mars only 22 kilometres wide.
Artificial satellites: Aryabhata in 1975, the INSAT weather satellites and the International Space Station.
The Chandrayaan-2 orbiter goes round the Moon. So it is a satellite of a satellite.
explanations.art: The Earth with the Moon far off on one side, and close to the Earth a space station and a satellite with a dish, each on its own ring.

explanations.concept: Two worlds both go round their balance point
explanations.definition: Two bodies held by gravity both go round one point between them, called the balance point or barycentre. The point lies nearer the heavier body.
explanations.description: In The Two-Ball Balance, you balanced a heavy dough ball and a light dough ball on a pencil. The pencil balanced at a point nearer the heavy ball. A ball twice as heavy sat half as far from the point. Worlds follow the same rule. The Earth has 81 times the mass of the Moon. So the Earth is 81 times nearer to their balance point than the Moon is. That puts the point about 4,700 kilometres from the Earth's centre, which is inside the Earth. The Moon goes round this point in a wide circle. The Earth goes round it too, in a small circle, once every 27 days. The Sun and Jupiter also share a balance point. It lies just outside the Sun's surface.
examples: The Earth and the Moon: the balance point is inside the Earth, about 1,700 kilometres below the ground.
Pluto and its moon Charon: the balance point is in the empty space between them, so both circle a point outside Pluto.
The Sun and Jupiter: the balance point is about 46,000 kilometres above the Sun's surface.
explanations.art: A big ball and a small ball joined by a faint line, with a cross on the line close to the big ball, a small circle drawn round the cross for the big ball's path and a wide circle for the small ball's path.

explanations.concept: What counts as a planet: the three tests of 2006
explanations.definition: In 2006 the International Astronomical Union agreed three tests. A planet goes round the Sun, is heavy enough to have pulled itself round, and has cleared other bodies from its path.
explanations.description: Pluto passes the first two tests. It goes round the Sun, and it is round. It fails the third, because it shares its path with thousands of icy bodies in the Kuiper belt. So since 24 August 2006, Pluto has been called a dwarf planet. Nothing about Pluto changed that day. The way people sort worlds changed. Many scientists who study planets still disagree with the third test, and the argument goes on.
examples: The Earth passes all three tests. It is far heavier than everything else near its path put together.
Ceres goes round the Sun and is round, but it shares the asteroid belt with millions of rocks. So it is a dwarf planet.
The Moon is round, but it goes round the Earth. So it is a satellite and fails the first test.

perspectives.who: Mike Brown, an American astronomer whose team found Eris in 2005
perspectives.explanation: The eight planets are far heavier than everything else near their paths. Pluto is one of thousands of similar icy bodies. Calling eight worlds planets shows a real difference in how the solar system is built.

perspectives.who: Alan Stern, the American scientist who led the New Horizons mission to Pluto
perspectives.explanation: A planet should be judged by what it is, not by where it is. Pluto is round and has mountains, glaciers, air and five moons. Any world heavy enough to be round should be called a planet, even if that gives more than a hundred planets.

explanations.art: Three tick-boxes labelled 'goes round the Sun', 'is round' and 'has cleared its path', with the Earth getting three ticks and Pluto getting two ticks and a cross.

explanations.definition: A dwarf planet is round and goes round the Sun, but has not cleared its path. Asteroids and comets also go round the Sun, but they are too small to be round.
explanations.description: Astronomers list five dwarf planets so far: Ceres, Pluto, Eris, Haumea and Makemake. Ceres lies in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. The other four lie beyond Neptune. Eris is almost exactly as wide as Pluto and has more mass. Asteroids are lumps of rock and metal, and most are in the asteroid belt. Comets are lumps of ice and dust that come in from far beyond Neptune. In Round or Lumpy, every world under 300 kilometres wide was lumpy, and every world over 900 kilometres wide was round. Why are big worlds round and small ones lumpy? A big world has strong gravity, and it pulls every part towards the centre. A ball is the shape where every part is as near the centre as it can be.
examples: Round: Ceres at 940 kilometres wide, and Pluto at 2,377 kilometres wide.
Lumpy: Phobos at 22 kilometres wide, and the asteroid Eros at about 17 kilometres wide.
In between: Vesta, at 525 kilometres wide, is nearly round but not quite.
explanations.art: A row of bodies from small to large: a tiny lumpy Eros, a potato-shaped Phobos, a nearly round Vesta, then round Ceres and round Pluto.

explanations.concept: A true model uses one scale for sizes and distances
explanations.definition: A scale turns every real length into a model length in the same way. A model is true only if sizes and distances use the same scale.
explanations.description: In Marble Earth, Peppercorn Moon, 1 centimetre stood for 8,000 kilometres. The Earth became a marble 1.6 centimetres wide. The Moon became a peppercorn 48 centimetres away. On the same scale the Sun is a ball 1.74 metres wide, as tall as a grown-up. It stands about 190 metres away, at the far end of a long street. Jupiter is a ball about 17 centimetres wide, nearly a kilometre from the Sun. Neptune is a lemon about 5.6 kilometres away. Pictures in books cannot show this. They shrink the distances far more than the sizes, so the planets fit on one page.
examples: The Earth and the Moon: a marble and a peppercorn, 48 centimetres apart.
The Sun: a ball 1.74 metres wide, about 190 metres from the marble.
The nearest star after the Sun is about 50,000 kilometres away on this scale. That is further than the distance once round the real Earth.
explanations.art: A long straight street seen from above with a person-sized yellow ball at one end and a tiny marble near the other end, the distance between them marked 190 metres.

explanations.concept: A ball twice as wide holds eight times as much
explanations.definition: When a ball becomes twice as wide, it also becomes twice as deep and twice as tall. So its volume becomes 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 times as much.
explanations.description: In Twice as Wide, a dough ball 4 centimetres wide took 8 of the small balls that were 2 centimetres wide. A ball 6 centimetres wide took 27, which is 3 x 3 x 3. The same rule works for worlds. Jupiter is about 11 times as wide as the Earth. So about 11 x 11 x 11 = 1,331 Earths would fit inside Jupiter. The Sun is 109 times as wide as the Earth, and about 1.3 million Earths would fit inside it. The rule also works the other way. The Moon is about a quarter as wide as the Earth, but about 49 Moons would fit inside the Earth.
examples: Twice as wide: 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 times the volume.
Three times as wide: 3 x 3 x 3 = 27 times the volume.
Jupiter, about 11 times as wide as the Earth: about 1,300 times the volume.
explanations.art: A small ball, a ball twice as wide and a ball three times as wide in a row, with 1, 8 and 27 small balls stacked under them.

explanations.concept: Almost all the mass of the solar system is in the Sun
explanations.definition: The Sun holds about 99.86 percent of the mass of the whole solar system. Everything else together is less than 2 parts in every 1,000.
explanations.description: In A Thousand Grains of Rice, 1,000 grains stood for the mass of the whole solar system. All but about one and a half grains belonged to the Sun. Jupiter was about one grain. Every other planet, moon, asteroid and comet together made less than half a grain. The Earth was a speck too small to pick up. This is why the Sun's gravity rules the solar system. It is also why the balance point of the Sun and any planet lies in or near the Sun.
examples: The Sun has about 333,000 times the mass of the Earth.
The Sun has about 1,047 times the mass of Jupiter.
Jupiter has about two and a half times the mass of all the other planets put together.
explanations.art: A large heap of rice on a steel plate labelled 'the Sun', with one single grain set apart labelled 'Jupiter' and a few broken bits labelled 'everything else'.

explanations.concept: The Earth and the Moon: a planet with an unusually large satellite
explanations.definition: The Moon is about a quarter as wide as the Earth. No other planet has a moon so large compared with itself.
explanations.description: The Moon is 3,474 kilometres wide and about 384,400 kilometres away. That distance is about 30 Earths side by side. Lasers bounced off mirrors on the Moon show that it moves away about 3.8 centimetres each year. The Moon's pull raises the tides in the sea. How did the Earth get such a large Moon? The leading idea is that a world about the size of Mars hit the young Earth about 4.5 billion years ago. Rock thrown out by the crash gathered into the Moon. Moon rocks brought back by astronauts fit this idea, but scientists still argue about the details.
examples: The Moon is about one-quarter of the Earth's width and has one eighty-first of its mass.
Ganymede is wider than the Moon, but it is only about one twenty-seventh of the width of Jupiter.
Charon is about half as wide as Pluto. Pluto is a dwarf planet, so it is not counted here.

perspectives.explanation: A world about the size of Mars struck the young Earth, and the Moon formed from the rock thrown out. This explains why Moon rock is so like the Earth's outer rock.
Moon rock is almost too much like Earth rock for a simple crash. Newer ideas include a much harder crash, or several smaller ones. Nobody saw it happen, so the evidence is still being weighed.

explanations.art: The Earth and the Moon drawn at the right sizes and the right distance apart across a wide page, with 30 faint Earth-sized circles filling the gap between them.

explanations.concept: Where does the solar system end?
explanations.definition: There is no single agreed edge. The answer depends on what you measure. The choices are the last planet, the last icy bodies, the Sun's bubble of gas, and the reach of the Sun's gravity.
explanations.description: Neptune, the last planet, is 30 astronomical units from the Sun. The Kuiper belt of icy bodies reaches to about 50. The Sun also blows out a thin wind of gas in every direction. This wind makes a bubble called the heliosphere. The spacecraft Voyager 1 crossed the edge of the bubble in August 2012, about 120 astronomical units out. But the Sun's gravity reaches much further. Comets seem to come from a far shell of icy bodies called the Oort cloud. It may reach 100,000 astronomical units out. Nobody has seen the Oort cloud itself. Astronomers worked it out from the paths of comets.
examples: By the last planet: 30 astronomical units, at Neptune.
By the Sun's bubble: about 120 astronomical units, where Voyager 1 crossed in 2012.
By the Sun's gravity: perhaps 100,000 astronomical units, at the edge of the Oort cloud.

perspectives.who: A scientist who studies the Sun's wind
perspectives.explanation: The solar system ends where the Sun's wind stops and the thin gas between the stars begins. Voyager 1 crossed that edge in 2012.
The solar system is everything the Sun's gravity holds. By that measure Voyager 1 is still deep inside it. It will need about 300 years to reach the Oort cloud.

explanations.art: The Sun and planets as a tiny dot inside a bubble, the bubble inside a huge round shell of small icy dots, with a small spacecraft between the bubble and the shell.

explanations.concept: A wobbling star gives away hidden planets
explanations.definition: A star with a planet goes round the balance point it shares with that planet. From far away, the star seems to wobble.
explanations.description: In The Hidden Ball, the visible ball swung in a circle, and the circle was wider when the hidden ball was heavier. A star with a planet does the same. Astronomers cannot easily see a planet beside a bright, far star. But they can measure the star's small wobble. In 1995 Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz found a planet this way, going round a star called 51 Pegasi. Since then thousands of planets have been found round other stars. Someone watching our Sun from far away could find Jupiter the same way.
examples: The Sun moves round its balance point with Jupiter once in about 12 years.
The first planet found by a star's wobble: 51 Pegasi b, in 1995.
A heavier planet, or one closer to its star, makes a wobble that is easier to measure.
explanations.art: A star drawn three times in slightly different places along a tiny circle, with a faint small planet on the far side of a much wider circle.

explanations.concept: The Earth's two movements and its tilt
explanations.definition: The Earth spins once on its axis in about 24 hours, which gives day and night. It goes once round the Sun in about 365 and a quarter days, which is one year.
explanations.description: The Earth's axis leans about 23.5 degrees away from the upright line, where upright means at right angles to the flat surface of the Earth's path round the Sun. This tilt gives the seasons. The Earth's distance from the Sun does not. The Earth is nearest the Sun in early January, when north India has winter. It is furthest in early July, in the middle of the monsoon. The gap is only about 3 percent, so it changes the heat very little. Mars leans about 25 degrees, so it has seasons too. Each Martian season lasts about twice as long as one on the Earth, because a Martian year is 687 Earth days. Uranus leans about 98 degrees, so for years one pole faces the Sun. The spin also gives travellers a guide. Seen from India, the night sky seems to turn through the hours, because the Earth is turning under it. The stars seem to circle round one point in the north. The Pole Star, called Dhruva Tara in Hindi, sits almost exactly over that point, so it hardly seems to move. It is a star far outside the solar system, many times further away than any planet. People on land and at sea have used it for thousands of years to find north.
examples: Spin: one turn in about 24 hours, so every place has a day and a night.
Journey: one trip round the Sun in about 365 and a quarter days.
Tilt: about 23.5 degrees for the Earth, and about 25 degrees for Mars.
Guide: a sailor or traveller in the north who finds the Pole Star on a clear night knows which way is north.
explanations.art: The Earth at four places on its path round the Sun, with its axis leaning the same way each time, and the Sun's light falling more on the northern half at one place and on the southern half at the opposite place.

agreed.text: Eight planets go round the Sun in the same direction, on paths that lie almost in one flat sheet.
agreed.evidence: Astronomers have tracked every planet for hundreds of years. Spacecraft have visited all eight, and each arrived where the orbits said it would be.

agreed.text: The Sun holds about 99.86 percent of the mass of the solar system.
agreed.evidence: The time a planet takes to go round the Sun shows how hard the Sun pulls. The orbits of moons and spacecraft give the mass of each planet in the same way.

agreed.text: The Moon is about 384,400 kilometres away, and it moves away about 3.8 centimetres each year.
agreed.evidence: Apollo astronauts and Soviet rovers left mirrors on the Moon between 1969 and 1973. Scientists time laser flashes that bounce back from them.

agreed.text: A satellite can be larger than a planet. Ganymede and Titan are both wider than Mercury.
agreed.evidence: The Voyager spacecraft, and later Galileo and Cassini, flew past these moons and measured them.

agreed.text: Two bodies held by gravity both go round a shared balance point, and the heavier body moves less.
agreed.evidence: Isaac Newton showed it in 1687. Astronomers have measured the wobble of the Sun, of Pluto and of thousands of stars with planets.

challenging.claim: Pluto is a planet, and any world heavy enough to be round should be called one.
challenging.who: Alan Stern and many scientists who study planets
challenging.for: Pluto is round and has mountains of ice, glaciers, thin air and five moons. A name should describe what a world is like. Even the Earth could not clear a path as wide as Pluto's.
challenging.against: This rule would give well over a hundred planets, and large moons would count too. The eight planets are far heavier than everything else near their paths. Pluto is not.
challenging.context: This card is about the argument over Pluto, which was renamed a dwarf planet in 2006.

challenging.claim: The Earth and the Moon are a double planet, not a planet and a satellite.
challenging.who: The writer Isaac Asimov and a few astronomers
challenging.for: The Moon is very large compared with the Earth. The Sun pulls the Moon more than twice as hard as the Earth does. The Moon's path round the Sun always curves towards the Sun.
challenging.against: The balance point of the Earth and the Moon is inside the Earth. By the usual rule, that makes the Moon a satellite. Astronomers have agreed no official meaning for 'double planet'.
challenging.context: This card is about whether the Moon is truly a satellite of the Earth.

challenging.claim: A satellite is always smaller than a planet.
challenging.for: Every moon is smaller than the planet it goes round. Most moons are tiny.
challenging.against: Ganymede and Titan are wider than the planet Mercury. Seven moons are wider than Pluto. A satellite is named for what it goes round, not for its size.
challenging.context: This card is about the belief that moons are small and planets are big.

challenging.claim: The Sun stands still at the centre while the planets go round it.
challenging.for: The Sun holds almost all the mass, so it moves very little. For most purposes the picture works well.
challenging.against: The Sun goes round the balance point it shares with the planets, mostly with Jupiter. That point is often outside the Sun. The whole solar system also goes round the centre of the Milky Way.
challenging.context: This card is about whether anything in the solar system stays still.

challenging.claim: A ninth planet, several times heavier than the Earth, lies far beyond Neptune.
challenging.who: Konstantin Batygin and Mike Brown, American astronomers, in 2016
challenging.for: Several far icy bodies have paths that lean the same way. The pull of an unseen planet would explain that.
challenging.against: Nobody has seen such a planet, in spite of long searches. Other astronomers say the pattern may come from where telescopes happened to look.
challenging.context: This card is about whether the solar system has a planet nobody has found yet.

big_questions.q: Pluto did not change in 2006, but its name did. Does a name tell you about the thing, or about the people who chose the name?
big_questions.hint: Think of the three tests for a planet. Who wrote them, and could they have written other tests?

big_questions.q: The Moon goes round the Earth, and the Earth also moves in a small circle round the point it shares with the Moon. Can one thing pull on another without being pulled back?
big_questions.hint: Think of The Two-Ball Balance. The heavy ball also moved in a circle when the pair turned on its thread.

big_questions.q: On the marble scale, the Earth is a marble 190 metres from the Sun. Why does the Earth feel so big to us?
big_questions.hint: Think of how long a journey round the Earth takes, and how far you have ever travelled.

big_questions.q: If you had grown up on Ganymede, would you call Ganymede a moon or a world?
big_questions.hint: From Ganymede, Jupiter would fill a large part of the sky. The Sun would be a small bright dot.

big_questions.q: Scientists voted on what a planet is. Can a vote decide what is true?

story.title: Thirty Steps to Neptune
story.note: Venetia Burney was a real girl. On 14 March 1930, aged eleven, she suggested the name Pluto at breakfast in Oxford. Her grandfather Falconer Madan passed the idea to Professor Herbert Hall Turner, who sent a telegram to the Lowell Observatory. The name was announced on 1 May 1930, and her grandfather gave her five pounds. The clay walk in the University Parks, the words spoken at breakfast and what Venetia thought are imagined. So is her answer to the telephone calls in 2006. She said later that she was not sure why the name came to her.
text: On the morning of 14 March 1930, Venetia Burney was eating her breakfast and thinking about nothing in particular. She was eleven years old. She lived in Oxford, in England, with her mother and her grandfather.
Her grandfather, Falconer Madan, had looked after a great library for most of his life. He was retired now. He read the newspaper aloud at breakfast, whether anyone had asked him to or not.

"Here is something," he said, and he shook the page flat. "A new planet has been found, beyond Neptune. An observatory in Arizona, in America, has been hunting for it for years. A young man there has found it on his photographs." He looked over the top of the paper. "It has no name yet."
Venetia put down her spoon.

She was thinking of a morning the year before. Her teacher had taken the class to the University Parks with a bag of clay, and had set a big lump of it on the grass. "This is the Sun," she had said. "Now, one step for the Earth."

A girl took one step and pressed a tiny lump of clay into the grass. Mars went half a step further. After that the steps grew long. There were five steps to Jupiter and nearly ten to Saturn. Uranus took nineteen.

Venetia had been given Neptune. She counted thirty steps, right across the grass and in under the trees. When she turned round, the Sun was a brown dot far behind her. She could not see the Earth at all.

She had stood beside Neptune's little lump, in the shade, feeling slightly cold. So this is how far it is, she had thought. From here the Sun would hardly warm you. It would look like one bright star among the others.
And now the newspaper said there was a planet further out than that. It was further than thirty steps. By her reckoning it was out past the trees, in the part of the Parks where nobody walked.
She thought about what such a place would be like. It would be dark and very cold. Even at noon, the sky would look like night.

Venetia knew the old Greek and Roman stories well. All the other planets had names from them. Jupiter was the king of the gods. Mars was the god of war, and Neptune was the god of the sea. There was one more god, she remembered, who ruled a dark kingdom under the ground, where sunlight never came. He owned a helmet that made its wearer invisible. No planet had his name yet.
"Why not call it Pluto?" she said.
Her grandfather lowered the newspaper. He did not laugh. He had spent his life among books, and he knew a good name when he heard one. "Why not, indeed," he said.

That same morning he wrote a note to his friend Herbert Hall Turner, who was a professor of astronomy. Professor Turner was away in London, at a meeting where the astronomers could talk of nothing but the new planet. When he came home and read the note, he sent a telegram to the observatory in Arizona. It said that a small girl, Venetia Burney, suggested the name Pluto for a dark and gloomy planet.
Then, for weeks, nothing happened. Venetia went to school. Names arrived at the observatory from all over the world. Some people wanted Minerva, and some wanted Cronus.

At last the astronomers at the observatory voted, and every one of them chose Pluto. It helped that the first two letters, P and L, were the initials of Percival Lowell. He had built the observatory and begun the search, and he had died before the planet was found.
On 1 May 1930 the name was announced to the world. Venetia's grandfather gave her a five-pound note. That was a great deal of money for a girl of eleven.
Venetia grew up and became a teacher. For seventy-six years, children in every country learned nine planets. The last of the nine had the name she had given it at breakfast.

But the astronomers went on measuring. Pluto turned out to be small. It was smaller than our own Moon. Then, far out beyond Neptune, they began to find other icy worlds, one after another, on paths like Pluto's. One of them had even more mass than Pluto. Pluto was not alone out there, past the trees. It was one of a crowd.

In August 2006 the astronomers met and voted again. This time they voted on what the word 'planet' should mean. By the new meaning there were eight planets. Pluto was something else, called a dwarf planet.
Venetia was eighty-eight by then. People telephoned to ask her how she felt about it. She told them she had been largely indifferent to the argument.

Earlier that same year, a spacecraft had set off for Pluto. It carried an instrument built by students and named after her. The journey took more than nine years, and Venetia did not live to see the pictures.

The pictures showed mountains of ice, and a wide pale plain shaped like a heart. Pluto was going round the Sun, as it had done for billions of years, forty steps out and past the trees. The word 'planet' had changed. The world she had named was the same as ever.
story.epiphany: For the parent: there are two turns. The first is at the breakfast table. Venetia has walked the true distances, so she can picture how dark a world beyond Neptune must be, and the name follows. The second is in 2006. The astronomers change the meaning of a word, and Pluto does not change at all. The story shows what a scale model is for. It also shows that 'planet' is a label people chose.
ask: Why did walking thirty steps help Venetia picture the new planet better than a drawing in a book could?
From as far away as Neptune, why would the Sun look like a bright star?
What did astronomers find beyond Neptune that made them think again about Pluto?
In 2006, what changed: Pluto, or the meaning of a word? How do you know?
If you could name a new world, what would you want to know about it first?

how_we_found_out.context: How did people decide which worlds to call planets? This card tells the true story, and an idea about Pluto that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: On 1 January 1801, Giuseppe Piazzi, an astronomer in Palermo in Italy, found a new world between Mars and Jupiter. He named it Ceres, and books listed it as a planet. Then more small worlds were found in the same region. By the 1850s there were many, and astronomers moved them all to a new list, the asteroids. In 1930 Clyde Tombaugh, at the Lowell Observatory in the United States, found Pluto. Astronomers expected a large planet, heavier than the Earth, because Percival Lowell had predicted one. The sums behind his prediction were done by his team of human computers, led by the mathematician Elizabeth Williams. But that expectation was wrong. In 1978 James Christy found Pluto's moon, Charon. The moon's orbit let astronomers weigh Pluto. It had only about 2 parts in 1,000 of the Earth's mass. From 1992, more icy worlds were found beyond Neptune. In 2005 Mike Brown, Chad Trujillo and David Rabinowitz found Eris, which has more mass than Pluto. Either Eris was a tenth planet, or Pluto was not a planet. On 24 August 2006, in Prague, astronomers voted for three tests, and Pluto became a dwarf planet.
how_we_found_out.who: Giuseppe Piazzi, Clyde Tombaugh, James Christy, and Mike Brown with Chad Trujillo and David Rabinowitz
how_we_found_out.when: Ceres was found in 1801 and Pluto in 1930. Charon was found in 1978 and Eris in 2005. The vote was on 24 August 2006.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That Pluto was a large planet, heavier than the Earth. In 1978 the orbit of its moon Charon showed that Pluto has only about 2 parts in 1,000 of the Earth's mass.
how_we_found_out.art: A young man in 1930 looking into a large brass machine that holds two glass photographs of stars, with a tiny arrow marking one dot that has moved.

roots.context: We have learned what planets and satellites are, how far apart they are, and that two worlds both go round a balance point. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In The Two-Ball Balance, the pencil balanced close to the heavy ball. When the pair turned on its thread, both balls went round that point, and the heavy one made the smaller circle. The Earth and the Moon go round such a point, and so do the Sun and Jupiter. So nothing in the solar system stays still while the rest go round it.
deep_truth.habit: We say the Moon goes round the Earth, and the Earth goes round the Sun. These words make us picture a big body that stands still in the middle. But every pull of gravity works both ways. The big body moves too, only less.
deep_truth.evidence: In The Two-Ball Balance, the ball with 4 pieces still made a small circle when the pair turned on its thread. The Earth makes a small circle every 27 days, round a point about 4,700 kilometres from its centre. The Sun circles a point that is often outside its own surface, mostly because of Jupiter.

three.who_am_i: You live on a world that moves in several ways at once. The Earth carries you round the Sun, and round the balance point it shares with the Moon. You feel still only because everything near you moves with you.
three.what_is_life: The Moon and the Sun pull on every living being on the Earth. Each being pulls back on them, a very little. The tides that feed crabs and shore birds twice a day come from that pull.
three.what_is_this_world: The solar system has no fixed middle that stays still. It is the Sun, the planets and the moons, all pulling on one another with gravity and all moving.

roots.thread: The Sun, the planets and the moons all formed from one cloud of gas and dust. They are separate bodies now, but gravity still joins every one of them to every other. The Moon pulls the Earth, the Earth pulls the Moon, and both pull the Sun. So no body rules from a still centre. The many worlds move together as one system, and each pair of them goes round a balance point that the two share.

teachings.source: Nicholas of Cusa, On Learned Ignorance (1440), Book 2, chapters 11 and 12
teachings.teaching: The universe has no fixed centre. The Earth is not at the middle of everything, and it is not at rest.
teachings.link: Cusa reasoned this out a hundred years before Copernicus. The Two-Ball Balance shows a small part of it: even the heavy ball moved.

teachings.teaching: It moves, and it moves not. It is far, and it is near. It is inside all this, and it is outside all this.
teachings.link: The verse speaks of the one Self, not of planets. Science finds no body that stands still. The sages say there is a stillness of another kind, which holds all movement.

teachings.source: Ernst Mach, The Science of Mechanics (1883), chapter 2
teachings.teaching: We can only say that one thing moves compared with other things. Nobody can point to a place that is truly at rest.
teachings.link: When we say the Earth goes round the Sun, we have chosen to treat the Sun as still. A balance point is a better choice than the Sun, but it also moves, round the centre of the galaxy.

science.text: Two bodies held by gravity both go round their shared balance point. Isaac Newton showed in 1687 that the Sun itself is always moving for this reason.
The Moon formed when a world about the size of Mars struck the young Earth. If so, the Moon is made partly of the young Earth's own rock.

other_view.view: The Sun holds 99.86 percent of the mass, and its wobble is tiny beside the orbits of the planets. Saying that the planets go round the Sun is true enough for almost every purpose. Talking a great deal about the balance point can make a small correction sound like a completely new picture of the solar system.

practice.title: Pulled and pulling
practice.say: Stand facing each other and hold each other's wrists. Lean back slowly, both together, until your arms are straight. Stay there for three slow breaths. Feel that each of you is holding the other up. Now turn slowly, a quarter of a circle, and notice whose feet move further. Then stand up straight and let go gently.
practice.kid: Hold a heavy book flat on your palm. Feel the Earth pull the book down. The book pulls the Earth too, just as hard. Take three slow breaths. Feel both pulls at once.

ask: In The Two-Ball Balance, even the heavy ball moved. Is there anything in your life that pulls on you without being pulled by you?
If nothing in the solar system stays still, what do we mean when we say 'sit still'?
Pluto's name changed and Pluto did not. Which of your own names and labels could change without changing you?
roots.art: Two children leaning back with straight arms, holding each other's wrists, with a small cross drawn on the floor between them and faint circles round it.

experiments.title: The Two-Ball Balance: where is the balance point of a heavy ball and a light one?
experiments.context: In this experiment you push a heavy dough ball and a light dough ball onto the two ends of a pencil. You find the point where the pencil balances on your finger. You change the heavy ball and look for a rule. You will find out how the balance point moves when one ball gets heavier.
experiments.question: A pencil has a heavy ball on one end and a light ball on the other. Where does it balance? How does the balance point move when the heavy ball becomes 2, 4 and 8 times as heavy as the light one?
experiments.predict: Guess first. With 1 piece of dough on each end, where will the pencil balance? Where will it balance with 2 pieces against 1, and with 8 pieces against 1? Why do you think so? Write your three guesses and your reasons.
experiments.fair_test: Use the same pencil every time, so the two balls are always the same distance apart. Cut all 9 pieces of dough the same size. Only the number of pieces in the heavy ball changes. Find each balance point twice, because a shaky finger can give a wrong reading.

materials.item: atta (wheat flour), 1 cup, with about 5 tablespoons of water, to make a stiff dough. Modelling clay also works
a long pencil, at least 15 cm, unsharpened or blunt. A chopstick also works
a ruler marked in centimetres
a butter knife
sewing thread, about 40 cm, and a small piece of sticky tape
a pen that can mark the pencil, paper and a plate

schedule.what: Make 9 equal pieces of dough. Guess. Balance pairs of 1 and 1, 2 and 1, and 4 and 1. Spin a pair on a thread. Find the rule and test it with 8 and 1.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for the three pairs. Then write the rule you found. Last, write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results, for a pencil 18 cm long
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished table can look like. The last column comes out a little under 2 and 4, because the pencil has some weight too. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A snake of dough 27 centimetres long on a table beside a ruler, cut into nine equal pieces with a butter knife.
setup.caption: 1. Roll the dough into an even snake 27 cm long. Cut it into 9 equal pieces.

setup.art: A pencil lying flat with a big dough ball pushed onto one end and a small dough ball on the other end.
setup.caption: 2. Push a ball onto each end, so each end of the pencil reaches the middle of its ball.

setup.art: A child's finger held out flat under the pencil, close to the big ball, with the pencil lying level across the finger.
setup.caption: 3. Slide the pencil along your finger until it stays level. Mark that place.

setup.art: A ruler held along the pencil, measuring from the mark to the end inside the big ball.
setup.caption: 4. Measure from the mark to each end of the pencil.

flow.do: 1. Mix 1 cup of atta with about 5 tablespoons of water. Knead a stiff dough that does not stick. 2. Roll the dough into an even snake 27 cm long. 3. Cut the snake every 3 cm, to make 9 equal pieces. 4. Measure the pencil and write down its length.
flow.say: We need nine pieces of dough that all weigh the same. An even snake cut every three centimetres gives us that. The pencil's length is the distance between our two balls.
flow.kid: Make a stiff dough. Roll an even snake 27 cm long. Cut the snake every 3 cm. You get 9 equal pieces. Measure your pencil.
flow.parent: The dough must be stiffer than chapati dough, so a big ball does not droop on the pencil. If the dough is soft, knead in a spoon of dry atta. Keep spare pieces under an upturned bowl.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Two-Ball Balance. Here you make 9 equal pieces of dough and measure the pencil.

flow.do: 1. Show how one ball will go on each end of the pencil. 2. Ask where the pencil will balance with 1 piece on each end. 3. Ask the same for 2 pieces against 1, and for 8 against 1. 4. Write down the three guesses and the reasons.
flow.say: Where will the pencil balance with one piece on each end? What about two pieces against one? And eight against one? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Where will the pencil balance with 1 piece on each end? Where with 2 against 1? Where with 8 against 1? Say why. Write your guesses.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: With equal balls it will balance in the middle.
The balance point will move towards the heavy ball.
With 2 against 1 it will be a little nearer the heavy ball. (A fair guess. The test will show how much.)

flow.context: This step of The Two-Ball Balance is for guessing. You guess where a pencil with two dough balls will balance, and say why.

flow.do: 1. Roll 1 piece into a ball and push it onto one end of the pencil. Stop when the end reaches the middle of the ball. 2. Do the same at the other end. 3. Rest the pencil across one finger and slide it until it stays level. 4. Mark the pencil at your finger. Measure from the mark to each end. 5. Do it once more and write both pairs of numbers.
flow.say: This is pair A, one piece against one piece. Slide the pencil slowly until it stays level. We do it twice, because a shaky finger can fool us.
flow.kid: Push one small ball onto each end. Rest the pencil on one finger. Slide it until it stays level. Mark the place. Measure to each end. Do it twice.
flow.parent: Squeeze each ball firmly round the pencil. Pair A should balance at the middle of the pencil. If it is more than half a centimetre off, the two pieces are not equal. Pinch a little dough from one to the other.
flow.context: This step of The Two-Ball Balance tests pair A, with 1 piece of dough on each end. You find and measure the balance point.

flow.do: 1. Add 1 more piece to one ball and roll it round again. This is pair B, 2 pieces against 1. 2. Find the balance point twice and measure to each end. 3. Add 2 more pieces to the heavy ball. This is pair C, 4 against 1. Measure again. 4. For each pair, divide the long part by the short part. Write the answers in the table.
flow.say: Now the heavy ball has two pieces. Which way has the balance point moved? How many times as long is the long part as the short part?
flow.kid: Add 1 piece to one ball. Now it is 2 against 1. Find the balance point. Measure both parts. Then make it 4 against 1. Measure again. Divide the long part by the short part.

ask.q: What happens to the balance point each time the heavy ball gets heavier?
good: It moves nearer the heavy ball.
When the ball is twice as heavy, the short part is about half the long part.

flow.parent: Each time, push the pencil end to the middle of the bigger ball again. With an 18 cm pencil, expect about 6 cm and 12 cm for pair B. Expect about 4 cm and 14 cm for pair C. Your numbers will sit a few millimetres nearer the middle, because the pencil has weight too.
flow.context: This is the main step of The Two-Ball Balance. You test 2 pieces against 1, then 4 against 1, and measure each balance point.

flow.do: 1. Keep pair C, 4 against 1. Tie the thread tightly round the pencil at its balance mark, and tape the knot. 2. Hold the thread so the pair hangs level. 3. Twist the thread gently and let the pair turn. 4. Look down from above. Watch the path of each ball.
flow.say: Watch from above while the pair turns. Follow the path of each ball with your eyes.
flow.kid: Tie the thread at the balance mark. Let the pair hang level. Twist the thread gently. Look from above. Which ball makes the bigger circle?

ask.q: Does the heavy ball stay still while the light ball goes round?
good: No. The heavy ball goes round the thread too.
The heavy ball makes a small circle and the light ball makes a big one.

flow.parent: Turn the pair slowly. If it tips, slide the knot a few millimetres towards the end that hangs low. The point to notice is that both balls circle the thread, and the heavy one makes the smaller circle.
flow.context: This step of The Two-Ball Balance hangs the pair with 4 pieces against 1 from a thread at its balance point. You turn it and watch both balls go round.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to say the rule in their own words. 2. Use the rule to predict 8 pieces against 1: divide the pencil's length by 9. 3. Add 4 more pieces to the heavy ball. Measure the ball's width and halve it. 4. Compare the two numbers. Then try to balance the pair with your finger right against the big ball. 5. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened.
flow.say: Tell me the rule you found. Now use it for eight pieces against one. Will the balance point be outside the big ball or inside it? Then tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why did it happen?
flow.kid: Say your rule. Divide the pencil's length by 9. Is that less than half the big ball's width? Try to balance the pair beside the big ball. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

ask.q: What rule joins the weights and the two parts of the pencil?
good: The ball that is twice as heavy sits half as far from the balance point.
Four times as heavy means a quarter as far.

ask.q: Why can you not balance the pair with 8 pieces against 1 on your finger?
good: The balance point is inside the big ball, where my finger cannot go.
Even with my finger against the big ball, the big ball still sinks.

flow.parent: Share the pencil's length into 9 equal parts for 8 against 1. The balance point is 1 part from the heavy ball's middle. For an 18 cm pencil that is 2 cm. The big ball is about 6 to 7 cm wide, so its surface is about 3 cm from its middle. After your child has explained, tell them this. The Earth has 81 times the mass of the Moon. Their balance point is inside the Earth, about 4,700 kilometres from the centre. The Earth and the Moon both go round it.

check.q: One ball is 4 times as heavy as the other. Where is their balance point?
options: 4 times nearer the heavy ball than the light one
At the very middle of the heavy ball
check.why: The heavy ball sits a quarter as far from the balance point as the light ball does. Choosing halfway means treating the two balls as equal. Choosing the heavy ball's middle forgets the light ball's weight, which always pulls the point a little towards it.

flow.context: This is the last step of The Two-Ball Balance. You say the rule you found, test it with 8 pieces against 1, and explain your results.

experiments.title: Twice as Wide: how many times as much dough?
experiments.context: In this experiment you make many small dough balls, each 2 centimetres wide. You join them into bigger balls and count how many it takes to make a ball 4 centimetres wide, then 6 centimetres wide. You will find out how much dough a bigger ball really needs.
experiments.question: A small ball is 2 centimetres wide. How many small balls does it take to make a ball that is twice as wide? How many for a ball three times as wide?
experiments.predict: Guess first. How many small balls will make a ball 4 centimetres wide? How many will make a ball 6 centimetres wide? Why do you think so? Write both guesses and your reasons.
experiments.fair_test: Make every small ball the same size, from equal pieces of one dough snake. Measure every ball the same way, between two upright books. Roll the big ball round each time before you measure, because a flat ball measures too wide.
results_table: How many times as wide as one small ball

materials.item: stiff atta dough from 1 cup of flour (the dough from The Two-Ball Balance can be used again)
a ruler marked in centimetres and millimetres
a butter knife
books with stiff covers, or matchboxes, to stand on each side of a ball
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Guess. Make 27 small balls, each 2 cm wide. Join them one at a time into a ball 4 cm wide, then 6 cm wide, and count. Find the pattern.

experiments.record: Write the width of the big ball after 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 27 small balls. Draw a line graph of width against the number of balls, or just read the numbers aloud to your grown-up. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: width of the big ball
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished graph can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A row of many small equal dough balls on a plate, with one ball standing between two upright matchboxes and a ruler across the gap.
setup.caption: 1. Make 27 small balls. Check that one is 2 cm wide.

setup.art: A child's hands pressing several small dough balls together into one larger ball.
setup.caption: 2. Join small balls one at a time, and roll the big ball round.

setup.art: A larger dough ball standing between two upright books, with a ruler laid across the gap showing 4 centimetres.
setup.caption: 3. Measure the big ball between two books. Count the balls used.

flow.do: 1. Roll one small ball of dough and show that it is 2 cm wide. 2. Ask how many such balls will make a ball 4 cm wide. 3. Ask how many will make a ball 6 cm wide. 4. Write down both guesses and the reasons.
flow.say: This ball is two centimetres wide. How many of these will make a ball twice as wide? How many for three times as wide? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: This ball is 2 cm wide. How many make a ball 4 cm wide? How many make a ball 6 cm wide? Say why. Write your guesses.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: Two, because the ball is twice as wide. (A very common guess. The test will show.)
More than two, because the ball also gets taller and deeper.

flow.context: This step of Twice as Wide is for guessing. You guess how many small dough balls make a ball twice as wide, and say why.

flow.do: 1. Roll the dough into a snake about 2 cm thick, as thick as a grown-up's thumb. 2. Cut a piece 1.5 cm long and roll it into a ball. 3. Stand a book on each side of the ball and measure the gap. It should be 2 cm. 4. Cut 26 more pieces of the same length and roll each into a ball.
flow.say: Every small ball must be the same size, or our count will mean nothing. Let's check the first one between two books before we cut the rest.
flow.kid: Roll a snake as thick as a thumb. Cut a piece 1.5 cm long. Roll it into a ball. Measure the ball between two books. Make 27 balls like this.
flow.parent: If the first ball is wider than 2 cm, cut the pieces a little shorter. If it is narrower, cut them a little longer. You may need two snakes. Twenty-seven balls use about two-thirds of the dough from 1 cup of atta.
flow.context: This step of Twice as Wide makes the small balls. You cut 27 equal pieces of dough and roll each into a ball 2 centimetres wide.

flow.do: 1. Press 2 small balls together and roll them into one round ball. Measure its width and write it down. 2. Add 2 more, roll and measure. 3. Go on adding 1 ball at a time. Roll and measure each time. 4. Stop when the ball is 4 cm wide. Write down how many small balls are in it.
flow.say: Two balls have gone in. Is the new ball twice as wide yet? Let's keep adding one at a time until it is four centimetres wide.
flow.kid: Join 2 small balls and roll them round. Measure. Add more, one at a time. Measure each time. Stop at 4 cm wide. Count the balls you used.

ask.q: Two balls did not make the ball twice as wide. Why not?
good: The new dough has to make the ball taller and deeper too, not only wider.
The dough spreads all round the ball.

flow.parent: Expect about 2.5 cm after 2 balls and about 3.2 cm after 4. The ball should reach 4 cm at about 8 balls. A count of 7 or 9 is normal. A ruler reads a soft ball only to the nearest millimetre or two.
flow.context: This is the main step of Twice as Wide. You join small dough balls one at a time until the big ball is 4 centimetres wide, and count them.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to guess again how many balls a 6 cm ball will need. 2. Go on adding balls. Measure at 12, 16 and 20 balls. 3. Add the rest, one at a time, until the ball is 6 cm wide. 4. Write down the count.
flow.say: Eight balls made it twice as wide. Do you want to change your guess for three times as wide? Why?
flow.kid: Guess again for 6 cm wide. Keep adding balls. Measure at 12, 16 and 20. Stop at 6 cm wide. Count the balls.
flow.parent: Expect about 4.6 cm at 12 balls, 5 cm at 16 and 5.4 cm at 20. The ball should reach 6 cm at about 27 balls. If your count is between 24 and 30, the test has worked.
flow.context: This step of Twice as Wide goes on to a ball three times as wide. You add small balls until the big ball is 6 centimetres wide.

flow.do: 1. Write the two counts side by side: about 8 and about 27. 2. Ask your child to look for a pattern with the numbers 2 and 3. 3. Ask how many small balls a ball 10 cm wide would need. 4. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened.
flow.say: Twice as wide took about eight. Three times as wide took about twenty-seven. What is the pattern? Now tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why did it happen?
flow.kid: Look at your counts, about 8 and about 27. Find the pattern with 2 and 3. How many for a ball 10 cm wide? Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

ask.q: What is the pattern?
good: 8 is 2 x 2 x 2, and 27 is 3 x 3 x 3.
A ball gets wider, taller and deeper together, so you multiply three times.

ask.q: A ball 10 cm wide is 5 times as wide as a small ball. How many small balls does it need?

flow.parent: After your child has explained, tell them this. Jupiter is about 11 times as wide as the Earth. So about 11 x 11 x 11 = 1,331 Earths would fit inside it. The Sun is 109 times as wide as the Earth, and holds about 1.3 million Earths.

check.q: A ball is 3 times as wide as a small ball. How many small balls of dough does it hold?
check.why: It is 3 times as wide, as tall and as deep, so it holds 3 x 3 x 3 = 27. Choosing 3 means counting only the width. Choosing 9 means counting two of the three directions.

flow.context: This is the last step of Twice as Wide. You compare the two counts, find the pattern and explain your results.

experiments.title: The Hidden Ball: can a wobble show how heavy a ball you cannot see?
experiments.context: In this experiment a helper hides one ball of a pair inside a paper cup. You watch only the visible ball and measure how wide it swings. Then you work out how heavy the hidden ball is. Astronomers find planets round faraway stars in much the same way.
experiments.question: A heavy ball and a hidden ball turn round their balance point. How does the width of the heavy ball's swing change when the hidden ball is heavier? Can you work out the hidden ball's weight from the swing?
experiments.predict: Guess first. When the hidden ball is heavier, will the visible ball swing wider, narrower or the same? Why do you think so? Write your guess and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: Keep the visible ball at 4 pieces of dough and use the same pencil each time. Only the dough hidden in the cup changes. Watch from the same place, level with the visible ball. Measure each swing twice.
results_table: Distance of the visible ball from the thread (cm)
My guess for the hidden pieces

materials.item: the pencil, thread and dough from The Two-Ball Balance
3 small paper cups with paper lids, or 3 small cardboard boxes, with sticky tape
a ruler or tape measure, and sticky tape to fix it on a wall
a helper, such as a parent, to hide the dough
a chair or a door handle to hang the thread from

schedule.what: Guess. The helper hides 1 piece, then 2, then 4 in a cup. Measure the swing of the visible ball for each. Work out the hidden pieces and open the cups.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for the three secret pairs. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results, for a pencil 18 cm long and a visible ball of 4 pieces
cols: Distance of the visible ball from the thread (cm)
My guess for the hidden pieces
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished table can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A parent behind a chair pushing dough pieces into a closed paper cup taped to the end of a pencil, while a child looks away.
setup.caption: 1. A helper hides 1, 2 or 4 pieces of dough in a cup on one end of the pencil.

setup.art: A pencil hanging level from a thread, with a dough ball on one end and a taped paper cup on the other, in front of a wall with a ruler taped across it.
setup.caption: 2. Hang the pair from its balance point, in front of a ruler on the wall.

setup.art: A child sitting two metres away, looking along the pencil's level, and marking on a notepad the far left and far right places the dough ball reaches.
setup.caption: 3. Twist the pair and let it turn. Mark the far left and far right places of the visible ball.

flow.do: 1. Show the pencil with a ball of 4 pieces on one end. 2. Say that a cup will hide a second ball on the other end. 3. Ask how the visible ball will move, if the hidden ball is heavy and if it is light. 4. Write down the guess and the reason.
flow.say: A cup will hide a second ball. You will see only this ball. Will it swing wider or narrower if the hidden ball is heavier? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A cup will hide a second ball. Will the visible ball swing wider if the hidden ball is heavier? Say why. Write your guess.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: A heavy ball pulls the balance point towards itself, so the visible ball is further out.
The visible ball swings in a bigger circle when its partner is heavy.
It swings less, because a heavy partner holds it still. (A fair guess. The test will show.)

flow.context: This step of The Hidden Ball is for guessing. You guess how a visible ball moves when a hidden ball of unknown weight is tied to the same pencil.

flow.do: 1. Tape the ruler flat on the wall, at the height of the visible ball. 2. Send your child out of the room. 3. Put 1 piece of dough in a cup, close it, and tape it to the pencil end. 4. Slide the pencil across your finger until it balances. Tie the thread there.
flow.say: Please wait outside while I hide the dough. I will call you in when the pair is ready. Do not look at the cup until I say.
flow.kid: Wait outside the room while your grown-up hides some dough in a cup. Do not peek.
flow.parent: Pair A has 1 piece in the cup. With an 18 cm pencil, the thread goes about 3.6 cm from the visible ball. Use the smallest, lightest cups. A cup weighs a few grams, so pair A may swing up to 8 cm. Hang the thread from a chair back or a door handle, so the pencil hangs level.
flow.context: This step of The Hidden Ball sets up the first secret pair, with 1 piece of dough hidden in the cup.

flow.do: 1. Call your child in. They sit about 2 metres away, level with the visible ball. 2. Twist the thread about 5 turns and let the pair turn. 3. Your child marks the far left and the far right place of the visible ball against the ruler. 4. They measure the width between the two marks, twice.
flow.say: Watch only the visible ball, with the ruler behind it. Where does it reach on the far left, and on the far right? How wide is the swing?
flow.kid: Sit 2 metres away. Watch the visible ball. Mark its far left and far right places. Measure the width. Do it twice.

ask.q: What is the width of the swing? Half of it is how far the visible ball is from the thread.
good: About 7 cm, so the ball is about 3.5 cm from the thread.
A small swing, because the hidden ball is light.

flow.parent: Stand behind your child and spin the pair gently. If the pair tips, slide the thread a few millimetres towards the low end. Watch from the side. From above, the visible ball would trace a circle, and from the side it shows only the left and right swing. Expect a width of about 7 or 8 cm. If you have a phone, film the swing from 2 metres. Pause the film at the two far ends.
flow.context: This step of The Hidden Ball measures how wide the visible ball swings for secret pair A. Only the visible ball can be seen.

flow.do: 1. Your child leaves the room again. 2. Hide 2 pieces in the cup and tie the thread at the new balance point. 3. Your child measures the swing as before. 4. Do the same for 4 pieces. 5. Write both widths in the table.
flow.say: Here is the second secret pair, and then the third. Measure each swing the same way. Which swung widest? Which swung narrowest?
flow.kid: Wait outside again while 2 pieces, then 4 pieces, are hidden. Come back and measure each swing the same way.
flow.parent: Pair B has 2 pieces hidden. With an 18 cm pencil, expect a width of about 12 cm. Pair C has 4 pieces, and the width is about 18 cm. Pair C is the easiest to see, because the thread hangs in the middle of the pencil.
flow.context: This is the main step of The Hidden Ball. You measure the swing of the visible ball for secret pairs B and C, with 2 and 4 pieces hidden.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to put the 3 widths in order, from the narrowest to the widest. 2. Ask them to guess the hidden pieces for each pair. 3. Use this rule: half the width is the visible ball's distance. The rest of the pencil is the hidden ball's distance. 4. Open the cups and compare. 5. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened.
flow.say: Put your three widths in order. Use the rule from The Two-Ball Balance to guess the hidden dough in each cup. Then we open them. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.kid: Put your 3 widths in order. Guess the dough in each cup. Open the cups. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

ask.q: How can the visible ball tell you the weight of a ball you cannot see?
good: The balance point sits nearer the heavier ball, so the visible ball swings wider when the hidden ball is heavy.
The width gives the visible ball's distance, and the rule gives the weights.

flow.parent: Work one together. A swing of 12 cm gives 6 cm for the visible ball and 12 cm for the hidden ball. The visible ball has 4 pieces. The hidden ball has 4 x 6 ÷ 12 = 2 pieces. After your child has explained, tell them this. Astronomers cannot see most planets round other stars. In 1995 Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz saw a star swing a little and worked out that a planet was pulling it. They did this with light, not a ruler.

check.q: A star swings in a small circle. What does a wider circle suggest about a hidden planet?
options: The planet is heavier or further away
The planet is lighter and nearer
The star is lighter than the planet
check.why: A heavier or more distant planet pulls the balance point further from the star, so the star moves in a bigger circle. Choosing a lighter planet reverses the rule. In The Hidden Ball, 4 hidden pieces made a much wider swing than 1 piece.

flow.context: This is the last step of The Hidden Ball. You use the swing widths to guess the hidden dough, open the cups, and explain your results.

activities.title: Marble Earth, Peppercorn Moon: how far apart?
activities.context: This activity starts the unit. A marble stands for the Earth and a peppercorn for the Moon. You guess how far apart they should be, then work it out with one scale.

materials.item: a marble about 1.6 cm wide, or a ball of dough rolled to that size
a whole black peppercorn
a ruler or a measuring tape, at least 50 cm
small slips of paper and a pencil

activities.record: Take a photo of the marble and the peppercorn with the ruler between them, or draw them. Write the scale: 1 cm stands for 8,000 km.

setup.art: A marble on a table with a child holding a peppercorn a hand-width away from it, about to put it down.
setup.caption: 1. Put down the marble Earth. Put the peppercorn Moon where you think it belongs.

setup.art: A ruler laid from a marble to a peppercorn 48 centimetres away, with small paper labels beside the marble at half a millimetre and at 4.5 centimetres.
setup.caption: 2. Work out the true distance, 48 cm, and move the peppercorn there.

flow.do: 1. Put the marble on a table or on the floor. Say that it stands for the Earth. 2. Give your child the peppercorn. Say that it is the Moon at the right size. 3. Ask your child to put the Moon where they think it belongs. 4. Ask why, and mark the place with a slip of paper.
flow.say: This marble is the Earth, and this peppercorn is the Moon at the right size. How far from the Earth should the Moon go? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: The marble is the Earth. The peppercorn is the Moon. Put the Moon where you think it belongs. Say why. Mark the place.
flow.parent: Most people put the Moon a few centimetres from the Earth, because pictures in books show it that way. Do not correct the guess yet.
flow.context: This is the first step of Marble Earth, Peppercorn Moon. Here you guess how far a peppercorn Moon should be from a marble Earth.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child the scale: 1 cm stands for 8,000 km. 2. The Earth is 12,742 km wide. Ask your child to divide by 8,000. The answer is about 1.6 cm, the width of the marble. 3. The Moon is about 384,000 km away. Ask your child to divide by 8,000. 4. Measure 48 cm from the marble and move the peppercorn there.
flow.say: On our scale, one centimetre stands for eight thousand kilometres. The Moon is about three hundred and eighty-four thousand kilometres away. How many centimetres is that?
flow.kid: The scale is 1 cm for 8,000 km. The Moon is about 384,000 km away. Divide 384,000 by 8,000. Measure that many centimetres. Move the Moon there.

ask.q: How does the true place compare with your guess?
good: The Moon is much further away than I thought.
About 30 marbles would fit in the gap.

flow.parent: 384,000 ÷ 8,000 = 48. The exact distance, 384,400 km, gives the same answer to the nearest centimetre. The gap is about 30 Earth-widths. Let your child look at the two tiny things and the long gap for a moment.
flow.context: This step of Marble Earth, Peppercorn Moon works out the true distance. On the scale of 1 cm for 8,000 km, the Moon is 48 cm from the Earth.

flow.do: 1. The International Space Station flies 400 km up. On the scale that is half a millimetre above the marble. 2. Television satellites sit about 36,000 km up. Ask your child to work out that distance, and mark it. 3. India's Sun-watching spacecraft Aditya-L1 is 1.5 million km away. Mark that too.
flow.say: Astronauts on the space station are four hundred kilometres up. Where is that on our marble? Now work out where a television satellite sits.
flow.kid: The space station is half a millimetre above the marble. A TV satellite is 36,000 km up. Divide by 8,000. Mark that place.

ask.q: People say astronauts on the space station are far out in space. What does the model show?
good: They are very close to the Earth, half a millimetre above the marble.
Only the Moon missions went far away.

flow.parent: 36,000 ÷ 8,000 = 4.5 cm. Aditya-L1 is at 1,500,000 ÷ 8,000 = 187.5 cm, nearly 2 metres from the marble. That is about four times as far as the Moon.
flow.context: This step of Marble Earth, Peppercorn Moon adds artificial satellites. The marble Earth and peppercorn Moon are 48 cm apart, and you mark where satellites go.

flow.do: 1. The Sun is 150 million km away. On this scale that is 187.5 metres. 2. Name a place about 190 metres from your home, such as a shop or a street corner. 3. The Sun is 1,392,000 km wide. Ask your child to divide by 8,000 and change the answer to metres. 4. Ask your child to describe the whole model in one sentence.
flow.say: On this scale the Sun is about a hundred and ninety metres away. How wide is it? Is it bigger or smaller than you?
flow.kid: The Sun is about 190 metres from the marble. It is 1,392,000 km wide. Divide by 8,000. Is the Sun bigger than you?
flow.parent: 1,392,000 ÷ 8,000 = 174 cm, or 1.74 metres. That is a ball as tall as a grown-up. About 190 metres is a walk of two or three minutes.

check.q: On a scale where the Earth is a marble, where is the Moon?
check.why: The Moon is about 30 Earth-widths away, which is 48 cm for a marble 1.6 cm wide. Choosing a nearer place usually comes from book pictures, which draw the Moon close so it fits on the page.

flow.context: This is the last step of Marble Earth, Peppercorn Moon. With the Earth as a marble, you work out how far away and how wide the Sun is.

activities.title: The Towel Spin: who makes the bigger circle?
activities.context: In this activity a grown-up and a child hold the two ends of a rolled towel and turn slowly round each other. You find out whether the heavier person stays in one place.

materials.item: a bath towel or a dupatta, rolled into a rope
a coin and a ruler or measuring tape

activities.safety: Clear the floor of toys and furniture first. Turn slowly, at walking speed, and stop if anyone feels dizzy.
activities.record: Write how far each person's feet were from the coin, and who is heavier. Draw the two circles from above if you like.

setup.art: A mother and a child facing each other on a clear floor, each holding one end of a rolled towel and leaning back a little.
setup.caption: 1. Hold the two ends of a rolled towel. Lean back a little.

setup.art: The same two people seen from above, turning round each other, the child's feet on a wide circle and the mother's on a small one, with a coin at the centre.
setup.caption: 2. Turn slowly round each other. Put a coin where the middle of the turning is.

flow.do: 1. Clear a space on the floor about 2 metres wide. 2. Each of you holds one end of the rolled towel. 3. Ask your child who will move in the bigger circle when you turn, and why.
flow.say: We will turn slowly round each other. Will I stay in one place while you go round me? Who will make the bigger circle? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Hold one end of the towel each, with your grown-up. Who will make the bigger circle? Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Towel Spin. Here a grown-up and a child hold a rolled towel and guess who will move in the bigger circle.

flow.do: 1. Both lean back a little, so the towel is tight. 2. Walk slowly round each other for four or five turns. 3. Each of you watches the other's feet. 4. Stop. Put the coin on the floor where the middle of the turning was.
