flow.say: Lean back a little and walk round slowly. Watch my feet. Am I standing still, or am I going round too?
flow.kid: Lean back a little. Walk slowly round each other. Watch the grown-up's feet. Stop. Put the coin at the middle of the turning.

ask.q: Did the heavier person stay in one place?
good: No. The grown-up went round too, in a smaller circle.
The middle of the turning was nearer the grown-up.

flow.parent: You will find that you cannot stay on one spot without pulling your child off their feet. Your own feet trace a small circle. If two children do this with each other, the circles are nearly equal.
flow.context: This is the main step of The Towel Spin. A grown-up and a child turn slowly round each other, holding a towel, and mark the middle of the turning.

flow.do: 1. Stand as you were when turning. Measure from the coin to each person's feet. 2. Compare the two distances with your two weights. 3. Ask how this is like the Earth and the Moon.
flow.say: Look at where the coin lay. Is it nearer to the heavier person or to the lighter one? Measure to find out.
flow.kid: Measure from the coin to your feet. Measure from the coin to the grown-up's feet. Who was nearer the coin? Who is heavier?
flow.parent: If you weigh twice as much as your child, the coin should be about half as far from you. This is a rough test, so expect only a rough match. The Earth has 81 times the mass of the Moon, so its circle is 81 times smaller.

check.q: A heavy person and a light person turn round each other, holding a towel. Who makes the smaller circle?
options: Neither, because the heavy person stays still
check.why: Both go round the balance point between them, and that point is nearer the heavy person. Choosing 'stays still' is the usual picture of the Earth and the Moon, but the heavy one always moves a little too.

flow.context: This is the last step of The Towel Spin. After turning round each other, you measure how far each person was from the middle.

activities.title: A Thousand Grains of Rice: where is the mass of the solar system?
activities.context: In this activity 1,000 grains of rice stand for the mass of the whole solar system. You guess how many grains belong to the Sun and how many to the planets, then find out.

materials.item: uncooked rice, about 2 tablespoons
a steel plate and a small bowl
paper and a pencil

activities.record: Take a photo of the big heap, the one grain and the broken bits, or draw them. Say or write which is 'the Sun', 'Jupiter' and 'everything else'.

setup.art: Ten small equal heaps of rice grains on a steel plate, with a child counting grains into one heap.
setup.caption: 1. Count 100 grains. Make 10 heaps of that size, for 1,000 grains.

setup.art: One large heap of rice on a plate, with a single grain set apart and half a broken grain beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Take out 1 grain for Jupiter and half a grain for everything else. The rest is the Sun.

flow.do: 1. Count out 100 grains of rice into a heap. 2. Make 9 more heaps of the same size by eye. 3. Push the 10 heaps together. This is about 1,000 grains. 4. Say that the heap stands for the mass of the whole solar system.
flow.say: This heap is about a thousand grains. It stands for everything in the solar system: the Sun, the planets, the moons and the rest.
flow.kid: Count 100 grains of rice. Make 9 more heaps of the same size. Push them together. This heap is the whole solar system.
flow.context: This is the first step of A Thousand Grains of Rice. Here you make a heap of about 1,000 grains to stand for the mass of the solar system.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to share the heap between the Sun and everything else. 2. They push the grains for all the planets and moons to one side. 3. Ask why they chose that share. 4. Count or estimate their planet heap and write the number down.
flow.say: Push to one side the grains you think belong to all the planets and moons together. The rest is the Sun. Why did you choose that many?
flow.kid: Push the grains for all the planets to one side. The rest is the Sun. Say why you chose that many. Write the number.
flow.parent: Many children give the planets a third or a half of the heap, because pictures show eight large planets beside the Sun.
flow.context: This step of A Thousand Grains of Rice is for guessing. You share 1,000 grains between the Sun and all the planets and moons.

flow.do: 1. Push all the grains back together. 2. Take out 1 grain. This is Jupiter. 3. Take out 1 more grain and break it in half. One half is every other planet, moon, asteroid and comet together. Put the other half back. 4. The rest of the heap is the Sun. Ask where the Earth is.
flow.say: One grain is Jupiter. Half a grain is everything else that goes round the Sun. All the rest is the Sun.
flow.kid: Take out 1 grain for Jupiter. Break 1 more grain in half. Half is all the other planets and moons. The rest is the Sun.

ask.q: Where is the Earth in the rice?
good: The Earth is a tiny speck of the half grain, too small to pick up.
It would take about 330 Earths to make one grain.

flow.parent: The Sun holds about 998.6 grains of the 1,000. Jupiter is about 1 grain. Everything else together is a little under half a grain. The Earth is about three-thousandths of a grain.

check.q: About how much of the mass of the solar system is in the Sun?
check.why: The Sun holds about 99.86 percent of the mass. Choosing a smaller share usually comes from pictures that draw the planets large beside the Sun.

flow.context: This is the last step of A Thousand Grains of Rice. Out of 1,000 grains for the whole solar system, you find how many are not the Sun.

activities.title: Round or Lumpy: how wide must a world be to pull itself round?
activities.context: In this activity you study the real widths and shapes of 12 moons, asteroids and dwarf planets. You look for the width at which worlds become round, and you explain the ones that do not fit.

materials.item: small slips of paper for 12 cards
a pencil
a sheet of paper for a number line

activities.record: Keep the 12 cards in order of width. Write one sentence saying where round worlds begin, and one sentence about a world that does not fit.

setup.art: Twelve small paper cards on a table, each with a name, a width in kilometres and the word 'round' or 'lumpy'.
setup.caption: 1. Write one card for each of the 12 worlds.

setup.art: The same cards laid in a row from narrowest to widest, the lumpy ones shaded in one colour and the round ones in another, with a mixed patch in the middle.
setup.caption: 2. Put the cards in order of width. Lumpy cards go in one row, round cards in another. Look for where they change.

flow.do: 1. Write these 12 cards, each with a name, a width in kilometres, a shape and what it is made of. 2. Deimos 12, lumpy, rock. Eros 17, lumpy, rock. Phobos 22, lumpy, rock. Hyperion 270, lumpy, ice. 3. Mimas 396, round, ice. Proteus 420, lumpy, ice. Miranda 472, round, ice. Enceladus 504, round, ice. 4. Vesta 525, lumpy, rock. Ceres 940, round, rock and ice. Charon 1,212, round, ice and rock. The Moon 3,474, round, rock. 5. Ask at what width worlds become round, and why big worlds are round at all.
flow.say: These are twelve real worlds. Some are round like a ball and some are lumpy like a potato. At what width do you think worlds become round? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Write the 12 cards. Each has a name, a width, a shape and a material. At what width do worlds become round? Say why you think so.
flow.parent: Vesta is nearly round, with a flattened shape and one huge crater, so it is counted as lumpy here. The widths are averages, because a lumpy body is wider one way than another.
flow.context: This is the first step of Round or Lumpy. Here you write cards for 12 real worlds and guess how wide a world must be to be round.

flow.do: 1. Lay the cards in a row from the narrowest to the widest. 2. Move the lumpy cards up into an upper row and the round cards down into a lower row. Keep the order of widths. 3. Find the widest lumpy world and the narrowest round world. 4. Find the part where the two rows overlap.
flow.say: Is there one width where lumpy stops and round begins? Or is there a stretch where the two are mixed?
flow.kid: Put the cards in order of width. Put lumpy cards in an upper row and round cards in a lower row. Find the widest lumpy world. Find the narrowest round world.

ask.q: What do you notice about the row?
good: Everything under 300 km is lumpy and everything over 900 km is round.
Between about 400 and 525 km, round and lumpy are mixed.

flow.parent: The narrowest round world is Mimas at 396 km. The widest lumpy one is Vesta at 525 km. So there is no single line. There is a mixed zone from about 400 to 525 km.
flow.context: This is the main step of Round or Lumpy. You put 12 worlds in order of width and find where lumpy worlds give way to round ones.

flow.do: 1. Look at the mixed zone again, and this time read what each world is made of. 2. Ask why icy Mimas is round while rocky Vesta, which is wider, is not. 3. Ask which world still does not fit. 4. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they found, and why they think it is so.
flow.say: Mimas is ice and Vesta is rock. Which is easier to squeeze out of shape, ice or rock? Which world still does not fit your rule?
flow.kid: Look at the mixed zone. Read what each world is made of. Why is icy Mimas round and rocky Vesta lumpy? Which world still does not fit?

ask.q: Why are big worlds round?
good: A big world has strong gravity, which pulls every part towards the centre.
The pull is stronger than the rock or ice, so high bumps sink down.

ask.q: Which world does not fit, and what might explain it?
good: Proteus is icy and 420 km wide, but lumpy.
Perhaps it stayed very cold and stiff, so it never settled into a ball.

flow.parent: Ice gives way more easily than rock. So icy worlds become round from about 400 km, and rocky ones need to be wider. Proteus is the odd one. Scientists think it has stayed too cold and stiff to settle. On the Earth, the same contest limits mountains to about 9 km high. Mars has weaker gravity, and its tallest volcano is about 22 km high.

check.q: Why is a world 1,000 km wide round, when a world 20 km wide is lumpy?
options: Wind and rain wear the big world smooth
The big world's gravity pulls its bumps down
check.why: A wide world has enough mass for its gravity to beat the strength of its rock or ice. Choosing wind and rain forgets that most of these worlds have no air. Fast spinning would flatten a world, not round it.

flow.context: This is the last step of Round or Lumpy. You use what each world is made of to explain why some narrow worlds are round and some wider ones are lumpy.

activities.title: Fix the Picture: how wrong is the solar system in a book?
activities.context: In this activity you measure a picture of the solar system in a schoolbook or on a poster. You work out where the Sun should be if the picture used one scale, and you write an honest caption for it.

materials.item: any picture of the solar system that shows the Sun and the planets, in a schoolbook, on a poster or on a screen
a ruler marked in millimetres
paper and a pencil

activities.record: Write the two measurements, your working, and your honest caption for the picture.

setup.art: A schoolbook open at a page showing the Sun and eight planets close together, with a child measuring the drawn Earth with a ruler.
setup.caption: 1. Measure the drawn Earth, and the drawn distance from the Sun to the Earth.

setup.art: A child's notebook with a multiplication worked out, and under it a hand-written caption for the picture.
setup.caption: 2. Work out where the Sun should be. Write an honest caption.

flow.do: 1. Find a picture that shows the Sun and the planets together. 2. Measure the width of the drawn Earth in millimetres. 3. Measure from the middle of the drawn Sun to the drawn Earth. 4. Ask whether the picture uses one scale, and how your child could check.
flow.say: Is this picture true to scale? How could we check? Let's measure the Earth and its distance from the Sun.
flow.kid: Find a picture of the solar system. Measure the drawn Earth in millimetres. Measure from the Sun to the Earth. Is the picture to scale?
flow.context: This is the first step of Fix the Picture. Here you measure the Earth and its distance from the Sun in a book's picture of the solar system.

flow.do: 1. The real Sun is about 11,700 Earth-widths from the Earth. Multiply the drawn Earth's width by 11,700. 2. Change the answer from millimetres to metres, by dividing by 1,000. 3. The real Sun is 109 Earth-widths wide. Multiply the drawn Earth's width by 109. 4. Compare both answers with the picture.
flow.say: The Sun is about eleven thousand seven hundred Earth-widths away. If the drawn Earth is this wide, how far away should the Sun be drawn?
flow.kid: Multiply the drawn Earth's width by 11,700. That is how far away the Sun should be. Multiply the Earth's width by 109. That is how wide the Sun should be.

ask.q: Could the true picture fit in the book?
good: No. The Sun would be many metres away from the Earth.
If the page showed the whole distance, the Earth would be too small to see.

flow.parent: An example. If the drawn Earth is 5 mm wide, the Sun should be 5 x 11,700 = 58,500 mm away, which is 58.5 metres. It should be 5 x 109 = 545 mm wide, about half a metre.
flow.context: This is the main step of Fix the Picture. You use the measured width of the drawn Earth to work out where the Sun should be on the same scale.

flow.do: 1. Ask why the artist drew the picture this way. 2. Ask what a reader might wrongly believe after seeing it. 3. Your child writes an honest caption of one or two sentences for the picture.
flow.say: The artist had a good reason to draw it like this. What was it? What might a reader get wrong? Write a caption that tells the truth.
flow.kid: Why did the artist draw it this way? What might a reader get wrong? Write an honest caption for the picture.
flow.parent: A good caption says that sizes and distances are not on the same scale. It may add that the planets are really tiny and very far apart. The artist's reason is fair: a true picture would show eight dots too small to see.

check.q: Why do book pictures show the planets close together?
options: The planets really are close together
A true scale would not fit on a page
check.why: On any scale that fits a page, the planets would be specks too small to print. So artists shrink the distances far more than the sizes. The distances themselves are very well measured.

flow.context: This is the last step of Fix the Picture. After working out how far off a book's picture is, you write an honest caption for it.

games.title: Name the World: planet, dwarf planet, moon or something else?
games.context: This is a clue card game. Each card describes a world or a machine, without its name. You say what it is, and which kind of body it is. Then you turn the card over to check.

printables.title: 24 cards: a clue on the front, the name and kind on the back. Print on both sides, and match the backs

items.f: I make my own light and heat. I am 1,392,000 km wide. I hold 99.86 percent of the mass of the solar system.
items.b: The Sun. A star. It makes its own light, so it is not a planet.

items.f: I go round the Sun once in a year. I am 12,742 km wide and round. I am far heavier than anything else near my path.
items.b: The Earth. A planet. It passes all three tests.

items.f: I go round the Sun in 88 days. I am 4,879 km wide and round. I have no moon.
items.b: Mercury. A planet. It is smaller than two moons, Ganymede and Titan, but it goes round the Sun.

items.f: I go round the Sun in 225 days. I am 12,104 km wide, with a surface hotter than 400 degrees Celsius. I have no moon.
items.b: Venus. A planet. It is the hottest planet, hotter than Mercury.

items.f: I go round the Sun in about 12 years. I am 139,820 km wide. I have about 95 known moons.
items.b: Jupiter. A planet. It has more than twice the mass of all the other planets together.

items.f: I go round the Sun in 84 years. I am 50,724 km wide. I spin tipped almost on my side.
items.b: Uranus. A planet. It is an ice giant.

items.f: I go round the Sun in 165 years. I am 49,244 km wide. I am the planet furthest from the Sun.
items.b: Neptune. A planet. It is 30 times as far from the Sun as the Earth.

items.f: I go round the Sun in 248 years. I am 2,377 km wide and round. I share my path with thousands of icy bodies.
items.b: Pluto. A dwarf planet. It is round and goes round the Sun, but it has not cleared its path.

items.f: I go round the Sun between Mars and Jupiter. I am 940 km wide and round. I share my path with millions of rocks.
items.b: Ceres. A dwarf planet. It is the only dwarf planet in the asteroid belt.

items.f: I go round the Sun in about 560 years, far beyond Pluto. I am 2,326 km wide and round. I have more mass than Pluto.
items.b: Eris. A dwarf planet. Its discovery in 2005 helped bring on the vote of 2006.

items.f: I go round the Sun beyond Neptune. I am 1,430 km wide and round. I am one of the icy worlds of the Kuiper belt.
items.b: Makemake. A dwarf planet. It is round and has not cleared its path.

items.f: I go round the Sun beyond Neptune. I spin once in about 4 hours, so I am stretched like a rugby ball. My longest side is about 2,300 km.
items.b: Haumea. A dwarf planet. It is heavy enough to have been pulled round, and then its fast spin stretched it.

items.f: I go round the Earth once in 27 days. I am 3,474 km wide and round. I am about a quarter as wide as the Earth.
items.b: The Moon. A satellite of the Earth. It is one of seven moons wider than Pluto.

items.f: I go round Jupiter. I am 5,268 km wide, wider than Mercury.
items.b: Ganymede. A moon of Jupiter. It is the biggest moon in the solar system.

items.f: I go round Saturn. I am 5,150 km wide and wrapped in thick orange haze.
items.b: Titan. A moon of Saturn. It is wider than Mercury, and it is the only moon with a thick air.

items.f: I go round Neptune the opposite way to Neptune's spin. I am 2,707 km wide, wider than Pluto.
items.b: Triton. A moon of Neptune. Some scientists think it was once a dwarf planet that Neptune caught.

items.f: I go round Mars. I am about 22 km wide and shaped like a potato.
items.b: Phobos. A moon of Mars. Its gravity is too weak to pull it round.

items.f: I go round Pluto. I am 1,212 km wide, about half as wide as Pluto. The balance point of Pluto and me is in empty space.
items.b: Charon. A moon of Pluto. The two go round a point between them, so some scientists call them a double dwarf planet.

items.f: I go round the Sun in the asteroid belt. I am about 525 km wide, lumpy, with one huge crater.
items.b: Vesta. An asteroid. It is large, but it is not round enough to count as a dwarf planet.

items.f: I go round the Sun and come close to the Earth. I am shaped like a peanut and about 34 km long.
items.b: Eros. An asteroid. It is a lump of rock, much too small to be round.

items.f: I go round the Sun once in about 76 years. I am a lump of ice and dust about 11 km long. Near the Sun, I grow a long tail.
items.b: Halley's Comet. A comet. Its tail is gas and dust that the Sun's heat frees from the ice.

items.f: I go round the Earth once in about 90 minutes, 400 km up. People built me, and astronauts live in me.
items.b: The International Space Station. An artificial satellite. People made it, but it goes round the Earth as the Moon does.

items.f: I was launched in 1975. I was India's first satellite, and I go round the Earth. I am named after an astronomer who lived about 1,500 years ago.
items.b: Aryabhata. An artificial satellite. It was named after the Indian astronomer and mathematician Aryabhata.

items.f: I was launched in 2019. I go round the Moon. People built me to photograph its surface.
items.b: The Chandrayaan-2 orbiter. An artificial satellite of the Moon. It is a satellite of a satellite.

printables.title: Score sheet: one row for each card, two points for each card
items: My name for the world (1 point)
My kind: star, planet, dwarf planet, moon, asteroid, comet or artificial satellite (1 point)
Bonus point: the test or the fact that told me

rules: Shuffle the 24 cards and put them clue side up in a pile. Give each player a score sheet.
Read the top card aloud. Do not turn it over.
Every player writes a name for the world and its kind. Give a reason for your kind, using what the world goes round, and whether it is round.
Turn the card over. A right name earns 1 point. A right kind earns 1 point.
Add 1 bonus point if your reason names the test or the fact that decides the kind.
The player with the most points after the whole pile wins.
Playing alone? Go through the whole pile. A score of 40 out of 72 is good, and 55 is very good. Then play again, and try to beat your score.

setup.art: Twenty-four paper cards in a pile on a table, clue side up, with a child holding the top card and a pencil.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards. Put them clue side up in a pile.

setup.art: A child writing a name and a kind on a score sheet while another child reads a clue card aloud.
setup.caption: 2. Read a clue. Write the name and the kind of the world.

setup.art: A card turned over to show the name Pluto and the words dwarf planet, with a child ticking a score sheet.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over. Score a point for each right answer.

flow.do: 1. Say the three tests for a planet aloud. A planet goes round the Sun. It is round. It has cleared its path. 2. Say that a moon goes round a planet. 3. Cut out the cards and give each player a score sheet.
flow.say: A planet goes round the Sun, is round, and has cleared its path. A moon goes round a planet. A star makes its own light. Keep these in mind. They decide every card.
flow.kid: A planet goes round the Sun, is round, and has cleared its path. A moon goes round a planet. Cut out the cards.
flow.context: This is the first step of Name the World. You learn the three tests for a planet and prepare the cards.

flow.do: Play by the rules. Read each clue, write down a name and a kind, then turn the card over and score. Talk about any card that the players got wrong.
flow.say: Listen to the clue. Which tests does this world pass? What does it go round? Write the name and the kind, and then we check.
flow.kid: Read a clue. Write the name and the kind. Turn the card over. Score your points.

ask.q: Which clue told you the kind of world?
good: What it goes round.
Whether it is round.
Whether it shares its path with others.

flow.parent: Children soon see that the width of a world never settles its kind. Mercury is a planet, and Ganymede and Titan, which are wider, are moons. Let them find this out.
flow.context: In this step of Name the World you play the card game. You name each world and its kind, and then check.

flow.do: 1. Pick out the cards that fooled you. 2. Say which clue misled you. 3. Ask your child to say which card was the most surprising.
flow.say: Which cards fooled you? What did you think the world was? What clue should have told you?
flow.kid: Find a card that fooled you. Say which clue misled you.

check.q: A world is round, goes round the Sun, and shares its path with thousands of icy bodies. What is it?
check.why: It goes round the Sun and is round, but it has not cleared its path. That is a dwarf planet, like Pluto. Calling it a planet forgets the third test.

flow.context: This is the last step of Name the World. You look again at the cards that fooled you, and say why.

games.title: Inside or Outside? Where does each pair balance?
games.context: This is a card game about balance points. Each card names two bodies that go round each other. You guess if their balance point is inside the heavier body or out in empty space. Then you work it out.

printables.title: 10 cards: a pair of bodies on the front, the working and the answer on the back. Print on both sides, and match the backs

items.f: THE EARTH AND THE MOON. The Earth has 81 times the mass of the Moon. Their centres are 384,400 km apart. The Earth's radius is 6,371 km. Inside the Earth, or in empty space?
items.b: 384,400 ÷ (81 + 1) = about 4,700 km from the Earth's centre. The radius is 6,371 km, so the point is INSIDE the Earth, about 1,700 km below the ground.

items.f: THE SUN AND JUPITER. The Sun has 1,047 times the mass of Jupiter. Their centres are 778 million km apart. The Sun's radius is 696,000 km. Inside the Sun, or in empty space?
items.b: 778,000,000 ÷ 1,048 = about 742,000 km from the Sun's centre. The radius is 696,000 km, so the point is OUTSIDE the Sun, about 46,000 km above its surface.

items.f: PLUTO AND CHARON. Pluto has 8 times the mass of Charon. Their centres are 19,600 km apart. Pluto's radius is 1,188 km. Inside Pluto, or in empty space?
items.b: 19,600 ÷ 9 = about 2,180 km from Pluto's centre. The radius is 1,188 km, so the point is OUTSIDE Pluto, about 990 km above its surface.

items.f: THE SUN AND THE EARTH. The Sun has 333,000 times the mass of the Earth. Their centres are 150 million km apart. The Sun's radius is 696,000 km. Inside the Sun, or in empty space?
items.b: 150,000,000 ÷ 333,001 = about 450 km from the Sun's centre. The radius is 696,000 km, so the point is deep INSIDE the Sun.

items.f: SATURN AND TITAN. Saturn has about 4,200 times the mass of Titan. Their centres are 1,222,000 km apart. Saturn's radius is 58,232 km. Inside Saturn, or in empty space?
items.b: 1,222,000 ÷ 4,201 = about 291 km from Saturn's centre. The radius is 58,232 km, so the point is INSIDE Saturn.

items.f: SIRIUS A AND SIRIUS B. Two stars. Sirius A has twice the mass of Sirius B. They are about 20 astronomical units apart. Each star is tiny next to that gap. Inside a star, or in empty space?
items.b: 20 ÷ 3 = about 6.7 astronomical units from Sirius A. Each star is far smaller than that, so the point is in EMPTY SPACE. Sirius B is 13.3 units from the point.

items.f: A MOTHER AND HER CHILD ON A SEESAW. The mother weighs 60 kg. The child weighs 30 kg. They sit 3 m apart. How far from the mother is the pivot?
items.b: The mother has 2 times the mass of the child, so 3 ÷ (2 + 1) = 1 metre from the mother. The pivot sits nearer the heavier person.

items.f: MARS AND PHOBOS. Mars has about 60 million times the mass of its moon Phobos. Their centres are 9,400 km apart. Mars's radius is 3,390 km. Inside Mars, or in empty space?
items.b: 9,400 ÷ 60,000,001 = 0.00016 km, about 16 centimetres from the middle of Mars. The point is deep INSIDE Mars.

items.f: JUPITER AND GANYMEDE. Jupiter has about 12,800 times the mass of Ganymede. Their centres are 1,070,000 km apart. Jupiter's radius is 69,911 km. Inside Jupiter, or in empty space?
items.b: 1,070,000 ÷ 12,801 = about 84 km from Jupiter's centre. The radius is 69,911 km, so the point is INSIDE Jupiter.

items.f: A PENCIL FROM THE TWO-BALL BALANCE. A ball of 8 pieces of dough is on one end, and a ball of 1 piece is on the other. The pencil is 18 cm long. The big ball is 6.5 cm wide. Inside the big ball, or outside?
items.b: 18 ÷ (8 + 1) = 2 cm from the heavy ball's middle. The big ball's surface is about 3.3 cm from its middle, so the point is INSIDE the big ball. That is why a finger could not reach it.

printables.title: Score sheet: a guess, a working and an answer for each card
items: My guess: inside or outside (1 point)
My working: the distance ÷ (the mass ratio + 1)
My answer: the distance from the heavier body's centre, to the nearest 100 km (1 point)

rules: Shuffle the 10 cards and put them front side up in a pile. Each player takes a score sheet, a pencil and a calculator or paper.
Read the top card aloud. Do not turn it over.
Every player guesses and writes: inside or outside. Then every player works out the distance. The rule is: the total distance divided by the mass ratio plus 1.
Compare the distance with the radius on the card. If the distance is bigger than the radius, the point is outside the heavy body.
Turn the card over to check. A right guess earns 1 point. An answer within 10 percent of the card's answer earns 1 point.
The player with the most points after 10 cards wins.
Playing alone? Guess each card first, then work it out and check. Try to guess right on at least 7 cards.

setup.art: Ten paper cards in a pile on a table, with a child reading the top card, a calculator and a score sheet beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the 10 cards. Read the top card. Do not turn it over.

setup.art: A child writing the word inside or outside, and then dividing 384,400 by 82 on a notepad.
setup.caption: 2. Guess inside or outside. Then work out the distance.

setup.art: A card turned over showing the working, with a ruler marking the Earth's radius and a cross marking the balance point inside it.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over and check your answer.

flow.do: 1. Remind your child of the rule from The Two-Ball Balance. A ball twice as heavy sits half as far from the balance point. 2. Say how to find the balance point: divide the total distance by the mass ratio plus 1. 3. Work the first card together, but do not turn it over until you have written a guess.
flow.say: A body 81 times as heavy sits 81 times nearer to the balance point. So the balance point is the total distance divided by 82 away from the heavy body. Let us try the first card. Do you think the point is inside the Earth?
flow.kid: Take the top card. Guess if the point is inside the heavy body. Then divide the distance by the ratio plus 1.
flow.parent: The Two-Ball Balance gave a pencil that balanced at 6 cm and 12 cm when one ball was twice as heavy. The total length was 18 cm. 18 ÷ (2 + 1) = 6 cm from the heavy ball. The rule is the same one.
flow.context: This is the first step of Inside or Outside. You learn the working from The Two-Ball Balance and try the first card.

flow.do: Play by the rules. For each card, guess first, then work it out, then check on the back. Talk about any guess that was wrong.
flow.say: Guess first. Is the point inside the heavy body or out in empty space? Then work it out. Which cards surprised you?
flow.kid: Guess. Work it out. Turn the card over to check. Score your points.

ask.q: What do the pairs with the balance point in empty space have in common?
good: Their two bodies are not very different in mass.
The two bodies are far apart compared with their sizes.
Pluto and Charon, and the two stars, are close in mass.

flow.parent: Children often guess that a pair always balances inside the bigger body. Pluto and Charon, the two stars and the Sun with Jupiter show that this is not so. The point is inside the heavy body only if the gap is small compared with its size, or the ratio is large.
flow.context: In this step of Inside or Outside you play the card game. You guess and work out the balance point of each pair of bodies.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child which card was the most surprising, and why. 2. Ask what would have to change for the Earth and Moon's balance point to be outside the Earth.
flow.say: Which pair surprised you? What would have to change for the balance point of the Earth and the Moon to be outside the Earth?
flow.kid: Which card surprised you? Say why.

check.q: Two bodies have the same mass. Where is their balance point?
check.why: With equal masses, each is the same distance from the point, so it is halfway. Choosing 'beside the heavier one' forgets that neither body is heavier here.

flow.context: This is the last step of Inside or Outside. You say which pair surprised you and what would change a balance point.

projects.title: The Planet Vote: hold your own meeting of 2006
projects.context: In this three-day project your family or friends hold a meeting like the one in 2006 that decided what a planet is. You study the facts, take sides with real arguments, vote on three rules, and write down what you decided and why.

materials.item: the 24 cards from Name the World, or a list of 12 worlds with their widths
paper slips for 3 ballots for each person
a notebook and a pencil
3 or more people to vote: family, friends or a class

schedule.what: Test 12 worlds against the three tests. Make a table of what passes and what fails.
Each person picks a side and prepares one argument and one answer to the other side.
Hold the meeting. Vote on three rules, hear the arguments, vote again, and write down the result.

projects.record: Keep a table of 12 worlds and the three tests. Write your side's argument and the answer to the other side. After the meeting, write both votes and one sentence on why they differed.

setup.art: A notebook page with a table of twelve worlds in rows and three columns headed goes round the Sun, round and cleared its path, with ticks and crosses.
setup.caption: 1. Test each world against the three tests. Tick or cross each box.

setup.art: Two children facing each other across a table with notes, one holding a card that says Pluto, with a paper ballot box between them.
setup.caption: 2. Take sides and prepare an argument. Then hold the meeting.

setup.art: Several paper ballots in a bowl and a child tallying votes on a sheet with three rows labelled rule 1, rule 2 and rule 3.
setup.caption: 3. Vote on three rules before and after the arguments. Count the votes.

flow.do: Day 1. Choose 12 worlds from the Name the World cards, such as the Earth, Pluto, Ceres, Eris, the Moon, Ganymede and Vesta. For each, tick or cross: goes round the Sun, is round, has cleared its path. Note which worlds pass all three.
flow.say: Test twelve worlds against the three tests. Then tell me which worlds you think should be called planets, even if they fail a test. Why?
flow.kid: Pick 12 worlds. Tick or cross each of the three tests for each one.

ask.q: Which worlds pass all three tests?
good: Only the eight planets.
The Earth passes. Pluto fails the third test.

flow.parent: Only the eight planets pass all three. Pluto, Ceres and Eris pass two and fail the third. The Moon and Ganymede fail the first.
flow.context: This is day 1 of The Planet Vote. You test 12 real worlds against the three tests of 2006 and note which pass.

flow.do: Day 2. Each person chooses a side. Side A says that only worlds that have cleared their path are planets. Side B says that any round world that goes round the Sun is a planet. Each person writes one argument for their side and one answer to the other side.
flow.say: Choose a side. Write one reason that supports it. Then write what you would say back to the other side. Use a fact about a real world.
flow.kid: Choose a side. Write one reason. Write what you would say back to the other side.
flow.wait: Do this the day after you test the worlds
flow.parent: Side A can say that each of the eight planets is far heavier than all the small bodies near its path. Pluto is one of thousands. Side B can say that Pluto has mountains, glaciers, thin air and five moons, so it is a world. Both sides are real. Do not pick one for your child.
flow.context: This is day 2 of The Planet Vote. You take a side and prepare one argument and one answer to the other side.

flow.do: Day 3. Everyone votes on three rules, in secret. Rule 1: the three tests of 2006. Rule 2: any round world that goes round the Sun. Rule 3: keep nine planets, as people learned in 1930. Count the votes. Then hear each side's argument. Vote again. Count again and write the results.
flow.say: Vote for the rule you like best. Then we hear both sides and vote again. Did anyone change their mind? What changed it?
flow.kid: Vote on the three rules. Hear both sides. Vote again. Write down the results.
flow.wait: Do this on the third day

ask.q: Did a fact or an argument change anyone's vote?
good: Yes. A fact about Pluto's moons changed my vote.
No. I kept my vote, but I understand the other side better.

flow.parent: Rule 3 keeps a list without a reason. In 2006 only a few hundred astronomers voted in Prague. Many of the world's astronomers were not there, and some said later that the vote was too small to settle the matter. Ask your child if a vote can settle what is true.
flow.context: This is day 3 of The Planet Vote. You hold the meeting, vote on three rules before and after the arguments, and write down what changed.

challenges.title: An Honest Solar System on One Strip of Paper
challenges.context: This is a drawing challenge. In Fix the Picture, a picture of the solar system in a book showed the planets near each other. Here you design a picture that does not mislead.
challenges.problem: Show the eight planets and the Sun on strips of paper so that nobody is misled. A picture that draws sizes and distances on two different scales must say so. You may use as many strips as you like.
constraints: Join 4 sheets of A4 paper end to end for a strip about 1.2 metres long.
On the distance strip, 1 astronomical unit is 3.5 cm. Mark the Sun at one end and Neptune at about 105 cm.
Show each planet's size to one scale. Put the sizes on a separate strip, or in a table.
Write a caption that says what each scale is, and that the sizes and distances do not use the same scale.
materials: 4 sheets of A4 paper and sticky tape
a table of planet distances in astronomical units and widths in kilometres
general: Mark each planet's distance as a dot on the long strip, and write its name above.
Draw a second row of circles for the planets' sizes, on a scale of 1 cm for 10,000 km.
Add a table with each planet's distance and width.
creative: Fold the long strip like a concertina, so that it fits in a pocket and opens to show the gaps.
Tape the strip along a corridor or a street and walk it, with one step for each astronomical unit.
Use a string of beads, one bead for each astronomical unit, with the planets as knots.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own honest picture of the solar system. Say what it shows well and what it leaves out. Write a caption that tells the truth.

setup.art: Four sheets of A4 paper joined end to end on a table, with a yellow half-circle at the left end and small dots with names along the strip.
setup.caption: 1. Join the strips. Mark the Sun and the distance of each planet.

setup.art: A second row of circles in different sizes under the long strip, the Earth about 1.3 centimetres wide, with a small caption box.
setup.caption: 2. Add a row for the planets' sizes, and a caption that names both scales.

flow.do: 1. Remind your child of Fix the Picture. A book's picture of the solar system drew the planets close together. 2. Ask what a reader might wrongly believe. 3. Read the problem and the four constraints together.
flow.say: In Fix the Picture, the book's picture put the planets near each other. What might a reader get wrong? How could we draw it without misleading anyone?
flow.kid: A book's picture showed the planets close together. How could you draw it truthfully?
flow.context: This is the first step of An Honest Solar System. You look again at the problem with the book's picture from Fix the Picture.

flow.do: 1. Join four sheets of paper end to end. 2. Mark the Sun at one end. 3. Multiply each planet's distance in astronomical units by 3.5, and mark the dot. 4. Draw the planets' sizes on a second row. 5. Check each dot against the table.
flow.say: Mercury is 0.4 astronomical units from the Sun. Multiply by 3.5 to find its place on the strip. Then do the rest. Check each dot.
flow.kid: Join 4 sheets of paper. Mark the Sun. Multiply each distance by 3.5. Mark each planet.
flow.parent: Distances in astronomical units: Mercury 0.4, Venus 0.7, the Earth 1, Mars 1.5, Jupiter 5.2, Saturn 9.5, Uranus 19, Neptune 30. On the strip: 1.4 cm, 2.5 cm, 3.5 cm, 5.3 cm, 18.2 cm, 33 cm, 66.5 cm and 105 cm. The four inner planets will be crowded into 5 cm.
flow.context: In this step of An Honest Solar System you draw the planets at the right distances along the long strip.

flow.do: 1. Write the caption. It must name both scales. 2. Ask your child what the picture shows well and what it leaves out. 3. Compare it with the book's picture.
flow.say: What does your picture show better than the book's picture? What does it still leave out?
flow.kid: Write a caption. Name both scales. Say what your picture leaves out.

ask.q: What does your picture leave out?
good: The sizes are on another scale, so the planets look too small on the strip.
The planets' paths are circles, but the strip shows only a line.
It does not show moons or dwarf planets.

check.q: Why must a picture of the solar system name its scales?
options: Planets are drawn in the wrong colours
Sizes and distances may not use the same scale
The Sun is too bright to draw
check.why: A reader cannot tell how far apart or how big the planets are unless the picture says what scale each part uses. Without it, a picture can mislead.

flow.context: This is the last step of An Honest Solar System. You write a caption that names both scales and say what the picture leaves out.

challenges.title: A Double World: build a pair that balances in empty space
challenges.context: This is a building challenge. In The Two-Ball Balance, the balance point of 8 pieces against 1 piece lay inside the big ball. Pluto and Charon balance at a point outside Pluto. Here you build a pair like that.
challenges.problem: Build a heavy ball and a light ball that hang level from one thread, with the thread outside the heavy ball. The heavy ball must be at least 6 times as heavy as the light ball.
constraints: The heavy ball must have at least 6 times the mass of the light ball.
The thread must be at least 1 cm outside the surface of the heavy ball.
The pair must hang level for 10 seconds without touching anything.
Use a stick or pencil no longer than 40 cm, thread, tape, dough, coins and nuts or washers.
materials: dough, coins, steel nuts or washers
a stick, chopstick or pencil, and a ruler
a kitchen scale, if you have one
general: Use a longer stick, so the balance point is far from the heavy ball.
Make the heavy ball small, by packing it with coins or nuts instead of dough.
Keep the heavy ball only 6 or 7 times as heavy as the light one. A much lighter partner moves the point towards the heavy ball.
creative: Hang the two balls on opposite ends of a 40 cm stick, with a dense stack of coins as the heavy ball.
Use a stack of 6 coins against 1 coin, on a 25 cm stick.
Use 7 steel nuts against 1 nut, on a 30 cm chopstick or stick.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own double world. Take a photo of the pair, or draw it. Show where the balance point is, and write the two distances. Write the mass ratio and how far outside the heavy ball the point lies.

setup.art: A 40 centimetre stick with a small stack of coins taped on one end and a tiny dough ball on the other, hanging level from a thread tied a little way from the coins.
setup.caption: 1. Tape a dense heavy stack on one end and a light ball on the other.

setup.art: A close view of the thread tied to the stick in the gap just outside the coin stack, with a ruler measuring the gap from the stack's edge to the thread.
setup.caption: 2. Tie the thread at the balance point. Measure how far it is from the heavy ball's edge.

flow.do: 1. Read the problem and the four constraints together. 2. Ask your child what makes the balance point lie outside the heavy ball. 3. Let them choose how to build the heavy ball and how long the stick should be.
flow.say: In The Two-Ball Balance, 8 pieces against 1 piece balanced inside the big ball. What could we change so the point lies outside?
flow.kid: The point must lie outside the heavy ball. Plan how. A longer stick? A smaller heavy ball?

ask.q: What two things push the balance point outside the heavy ball?
good: A longer gap between the balls.
A small heavy ball, made of something dense.
A heavy ball that is not too much heavier than the light one.

flow.context: This is the first step of A Double World. You plan how to build a pair whose balance point lies outside the heavy ball.

flow.do: 1. Build the heavy ball and the light ball. 2. Tape each to an end of the stick, with its middle at the end. 3. Slide the stick across your finger to find the balance point. 4. Tie the thread there. Measure the distance from the thread to the heavy ball's edge.
flow.say: Build your pair. Find the balance point. Is the thread inside the heavy ball, or outside? How far outside?
flow.kid: Build the pair. Find the balance point. Tie the thread. Is it outside the heavy ball?
flow.parent: A stack of 6 one-rupee coins is small, about 1 cm tall and 2 cm wide. A single coin is the light ball. With a 25 cm stick, the balance point is 25 ÷ 7 = 3.6 cm from the stack's middle. That is about 2.5 cm outside the stack. The stick's own weight pushes the point a little further out. A dough ball of 6 pieces is too big for this, so use coins or nuts.
flow.context: In this step of A Double World you build the heavy ball and the light ball, and find where the pair balances.

flow.do: 1. Hang the pair by its thread. 2. Check that it stays level for 10 seconds. 3. Check the four constraints. 4. If it fails, change one thing and try again.
flow.say: Hang your pair. Does it stay level? Is the thread more than 1 centimetre outside the heavy ball? What would you change?
flow.kid: Hang the pair. Does it stay level for 10 seconds? Check each constraint.

check.q: A heavy ball is 8 times as heavy as a light ball. When is their balance point outside the heavy ball?
options: When the gap is more than 9 times the heavy ball's radius
When the gap is less than the heavy ball's radius
Never, because the heavy ball is heavier
check.why: The balance point is the gap divided by 9, measured from the heavy ball's middle. It is outside the ball when that is more than the ball's radius. So the gap must be more than 9 times the radius. Choosing 'never' forgets that a long gap moves the point out.

flow.context: This is the last step of A Double World. You hang the pair, check that it balances, and test it against the four constraints.

worksheets.title: Planets, moons and what each world goes round

items.p: Put these planets in order from the Sun, nearest first.
items.why: The order from the Sun is Mercury, Venus, the Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. The four rocky planets come first and the giants after them.

items.p: Match each body to the world it goes round.
items.why: A body is named by what it goes round. The Earth goes round the Sun, so it is a planet. Each of the others goes round a world that is not a star, so each is a satellite.

items.p: A body that makes its own light and heat is called a ____.
items.why: The Sun is a star. Planets and moons only reflect the Sun's light.

items.p: A moon can be wider than a planet.
items.why: True. Ganymede and Titan are both wider than Mercury. A moon is named for what it goes round, not for its size.

items.p: Ganymede is 5,268 km wide and Mercury is 4,879 km wide. What is Ganymede?
opts: A planet, because it is wider than Mercury
A moon, because it goes round Jupiter
A dwarf planet, because it is smaller than Jupiter
items.why: Ganymede goes round Jupiter, so it is a moon. Choosing 'a planet' uses width as the test. Width is not one of the tests.

items.p: Sort these worlds by shape. Is each one round or lumpy?
items.why: A world with enough mass pulls every part towards its centre, and becomes a ball. Phobos, Deimos and Eros are only 12 to 34 km wide, so their pull is too weak.

items.p: Which of these is NOT one of the three tests for a planet?
opts: It is heavy enough to be round
It has at least one moon
items.why: Mercury and Venus are planets and have no moon. The three tests are going round the Sun, being round, and having cleared the path.

items.p: In 2006, Pluto shrank, so it stopped being a planet.
items.why: False. Pluto did not change at all. Astronomers agreed on three tests for a planet, and Pluto fails the third one.

items.p: In The Two-Ball Balance, one ball had 4 pieces and the other had 1. Where did the pencil balance? Say why.
items.a: It balanced about 4 times nearer the heavy ball than the light ball. On an 18 cm pencil that was about 4 cm from the heavy ball and 14 cm from the light ball. A ball that is 4 times as heavy needs only a quarter of the reach to balance.
items.why: A strong answer says where the pencil balanced and gives numbers or a ratio. It says the heavier ball sits nearer the balance point.

items.p: Draw a pencil with a heavy ball on one end and a light ball on the other. Mark the balance point.
items.a: The heavy ball is drawn bigger. The balance point is marked on the pencil close to the heavy ball. The part of the pencil on the light ball's side is longer.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the balance point nearer the heavy ball. It shows two parts of the pencil, and the longer part is on the light ball's side.
items.art: A pencil lying flat with a large dough ball on the left end and a small dough ball on the right end, and a blank space for the balance mark.

items.p: A ball of dough is 4 times as wide as a small ball. How many small balls make it?
items.why: A ball 4 times as wide is also 4 times as tall and 4 times as deep. So it holds 4 x 4 x 4 = 64 small balls.

items.p: The Moon is about a quarter as wide as the Earth. About how many Moons would fit inside the Earth?
items.why: The Earth is nearly 4 times as wide, so the Moon fits in about 4 x 4 x 4 = 64 times. The true figure is about 49, because the Moon is a little more than a quarter as wide.

items.p: Should Pluto be called a planet?

views.who: A scientist who counts the worlds near each path
views.says: The eight planets are far heavier than all the small bodies near their paths. Pluto is one of thousands of icy bodies. It should be called a dwarf planet.

views.who: A scientist who flew a spacecraft to Pluto
views.says: Pluto has mountains, glaciers, thin air and five moons. A world like that is a planet, whether or not it has cleared its path.
A name is a tool for sorting. I would pick the rule that helps children see how the solar system is built, and change it if we learn more.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from a fact in this lesson. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a fact. One reason for the first: Pluto shares its path with thousands of icy bodies. One for the second: Pluto is round, has air and has five moons. One for the third: Eris, found in 2005, has more mass than Pluto, so the list of planets would keep growing.
items.why: A strong answer uses a real fact, such as the Kuiper belt, Pluto's moons or Eris. It treats the other views fairly. Scientists still argue about this.

items.p: Label each part of this drawing of the solar system.
a: The asteroid belt: the ring of rocks between Mars and Jupiter
The Kuiper belt: the ring of icy bodies beyond Neptune
A rocky planet: one of the first four from the Sun
A giant planet: one of the last four from the Sun
items.why: Mercury, Venus, the Earth and Mars are rocky. Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are giants of gas and ice. The asteroid belt lies between Mars and Jupiter, and the Kuiper belt lies beyond Neptune.
items.art: A long drawing of the Sun, four small planets, a ring of small rocks, four large planets and an outer ring of icy dots, with four blank label lines.

items.p: Three of these go round the Earth. Which one does not?
items.why: Ceres goes round the Sun, in the asteroid belt. The Moon is a natural satellite, and the other two are artificial satellites.

items.p: One world has 3 times the mass of its partner. How much nearer the balance point is the heavy world?
items.why: The heavy world sits as many times nearer the balance point as it is times heavier. With 3 times the mass, it is 3 times nearer.

items.p: Balls of 4 pieces and 1 piece sit at the ends of a 20 cm pencil. Where is the balance point?
items.why: The pencil is cut into 4 + 1 = 5 equal parts, and the balance point is 1 part from the heavy end. 20 ÷ 5 = 4 cm. The middle, 10 cm, is only right for equal balls.

items.p: The Earth stays still while the Moon goes round it.
items.why: False. Both go round their balance point. The Earth's circle is small, about 4,700 km from its centre, because the Earth is 81 times as heavy.

items.p: In The Towel Spin, the coin lay nearer the grown-up than the child. Explain why.
items.a: The coin marked the middle of the turning. The grown-up was heavier, so the middle was nearer to the grown-up. The child, who was lighter, went round in the wider circle.
items.why: A strong answer says both people went round one point. It says the heavier person sits nearer that point, and links this to the Earth and the Moon.

items.p: In the marble model, the Earth is 1.6 cm wide. About how wide is the Moon?
items.why: The Moon is about a quarter as wide as the Earth. A quarter of 16 mm is about 4 mm, the size of a peppercorn.

items.p: On a scale of 1 cm for 100 km, how many centimetres stand for 384,000 km, the Moon's distance?
items.why: 384,000 ÷ 100 = 3,840 cm, which is 38.4 metres. On this scale the Earth is 1.27 metres wide.

items.p: A picture that draws the planets big and close together uses one scale for sizes and distances.
items.why: False. Real distances are far larger than real sizes. A picture that shows both close together has shrunk the distances far more than the sizes.

items.p: A world is 10 times as wide as another and made of the same stuff. How much more material does it hold?
items.why: It is 10 times as wide, as tall and as deep. 10 x 10 x 10 = 1,000.

items.p: Match each world to about how many Earths would fit inside it.
items.why: The number of Earths is the cube of how many times as wide the world is. The Sun is 109 times as wide, and 109 x 109 x 109 is about 1.3 million.

items.p: Does each world go round the Sun, or go round a planet?
items.why: What a body goes round decides its group. Ceres, Mercury and Eris go round the Sun. Ganymede, Phobos and Titan go round a planet.

items.p: Put these in order, from the least mass to the most mass.
items.why: The Earth has 81 times the Moon's mass. Jupiter has about 318 times the Earth's mass. The Sun has about 1,047 times Jupiter's mass.

items.p: Ganymede is wider than Mercury. Yet Ganymede is a moon and Mercury is a planet. Explain why.
items.a: A body is named by what it goes round. Ganymede goes round Jupiter, so it is a moon. Mercury goes round the Sun, so it is a planet. Width is not a test.
items.why: A strong answer says that the name depends on what the body goes round, and says that size is not the test.

items.p: Where does the solar system end?

views.who: A scientist who studies the Sun's wind
views.says: It ends where the Sun's wind meets the thin gas between the stars. Voyager 1 crossed that edge in 2012, about 120 times as far from the Sun as the Earth.
It ends where the Sun's gravity stops holding bodies. Comets seem to come from a shell of icy bodies that may reach 100,000 times as far as the Earth.
I would draw the edge at Neptune. It is the last planet, 30 times as far from the Sun as the Earth.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. For the first: the wind is something that Voyager 1 could measure. For the second: the Sun's gravity still holds comets far beyond Voyager 1. For the third: planets are what most people mean by the solar system.
items.why: There is no single agreed edge, because the answer depends on what you measure. A strong answer says what is being measured and treats the other views fairly.

items.p: Draw the Earth and the Moon on a scale of 1 cm for 40,000 km. Show their sizes and the gap.
items.a: The Earth is about 3 mm wide. The Moon is about 1 mm wide. They are about 9.6 cm apart.
items.why: 12,742 ÷ 40,000 = 0.32 cm. 3,474 ÷ 40,000 = 0.09 cm. 384,400 ÷ 40,000 = 9.6 cm. A strong drawing shows a wide gap and two very small bodies.
items.art: A blank strip of paper 12 cm long, with a ruler marked along the bottom.

items.p: The balance point of the Earth and the Moon lies inside the ____.
items.why: The point is about 4,700 km from the Earth's centre, and the Earth's radius is 6,371 km.

items.p: The Pole Star is a planet that goes round the Sun, like Jupiter.
items.why: False. The Pole Star makes its own light, so it is a star. It is far outside the solar system. Travellers use it to find north because it hardly moves in the night sky.

worksheets.title: Testing ideas about the solar system

items.p: A new round icy world is found beyond Neptune, among thousands of icy bodies. What is it, by the 2006 tests?
items.why: It goes round the Sun and is round, but it has not cleared its path. That is a dwarf planet.

items.p: Seven moons in the solar system are wider than Pluto.
items.why: True. They are Ganymede, Titan, Callisto, Io, our Moon, Europa and Triton. Pluto is 2,377 km wide.

items.p: Two worlds with exactly the same mass have their balance point halfway between them.
items.why: True. Each world is as far from the point as the other, so the point is halfway. The balance point only moves towards the heavier one.

items.p: The Sun and Jupiter share a balance point just above the Sun's surface. What does this show?
opts: Jupiter is wider than the Sun
The Sun moves a little as Jupiter goes round
Jupiter does not go round the Sun
items.why: The Sun goes round the balance point too, in a small circle. It does so once in about 12 years, as Jupiter goes round.

items.p: In A Thousand Grains of Rice, the Sun has 998.6 grains and Jupiter 1. How many grains are left for everything else?
items.why: 1,000 − 998.6 − 1 = 0.4 grains. All the other planets, moons, asteroids and comets together are less than half a grain.

items.p: A drawn Earth is 4 mm wide. The Sun is 11,700 Earth-widths away. On that scale, how many metres away is it?
items.why: 4 x 11,700 = 46,800 mm. 46,800 mm is 46.8 metres. A page could never show that.

items.p: Uranus is about 4 times as wide as the Earth. Roughly how many Earths would fit inside it?
items.why: 4 x 4 x 4 = 64. The true figure is about 63, because Uranus is a little under 4 times as wide.

items.p: In The Hidden Ball, the visible ball swung wider when the hidden ball was heavier. Explain why.
items.a: The balance point sits nearer the heavier ball. When the hidden ball was heavy, the point moved towards it. That left the visible ball further from the point, so it went round in a wider circle.
items.why: A strong answer says the point moves towards the heavier ball. It links the distance from the point to the size of the circle.

items.p: Is the Moon a satellite of the Earth, or are they a double planet?

views.who: An astronomer who follows the usual rule
views.says: Their balance point is inside the Earth. So the Moon goes round the Earth, and it is a satellite.

views.who: A writer who argues for a double planet
views.says: The Moon is very large for a satellite. The Sun pulls the Moon more than twice as hard as the Earth does. So the pair is a double planet.
The name does not matter. What matters is the mass ratio, the distance and the balance point, and those are measured.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. For the first: the balance point is about 4,700 km from the Earth's centre. For the second: the Moon's size and the Sun's pull on it. For the third: the numbers are agreed, and only the name is argued over.
items.why: A strong answer uses a fact such as the balance point or the Sun's pull. Astronomers have never agreed an official meaning for 'double planet'.

items.p: Match each world to why it is not a planet.
pairs: It has not cleared its path
It is too small to be round
items.why: Pluto fails the third test. The Moon fails the first, since it goes round the Earth. Vesta is too small to have pulled itself round. The Sun makes its own light.

items.p: Put these in order, from nearest to furthest from the Sun.
items: The end of the Kuiper belt
The edge of the Sun's bubble
a: The end of the Kuiper belt
The edge of the Sun's bubble
items.why: Neptune is 30 astronomical units out. The Kuiper belt reaches about 50. The Sun's bubble ends about 120 out. The Oort cloud may reach about 100,000.

items.p: Nobody has seen the Oort cloud. How do astronomers know it is probably there?
opts: Comets seem to come from far away in every direction
Moon rock holds pieces of it
items.why: Astronomers worked out where comets come from by studying their paths. Voyager 1 will need about 300 years to reach the Oort cloud.

items.p: A planet with a heavier moon wobbles more than one with a lighter moon, at the same distance.
items.why: True. A heavier moon pulls the balance point further from the planet's middle, so the planet goes round in a bigger circle. This is how astronomers find planets round other stars.

items.p: Many people think the Sun stands still while the planets go round it. What would you tell them? Use a fact.
items.a: The Sun moves too. The Sun and Jupiter go round a balance point that lies just above the Sun's surface, once in about 12 years. Every planet pulls the Sun a little, so the Sun is never still.
items.why: A strong answer says that the pull works both ways, and uses a fact such as the Sun and Jupiter's balance point. It is fair about the idea: the Sun moves very little.

items.p: A model is true only if it uses one ____ for sizes and distances.
items.why: A scale turns every real length into a model length in the same way. A model with two scales can mislead.

quiz.p: Which is the largest of the four rocky planets?
quiz.why: The Earth is 12,742 km wide, a little wider than Venus at 12,104 km. Mars and Mercury are much smaller.

quiz.p: Which of these is true of the Earth and no other planet?
opts: It has seas of liquid water on its surface
quiz.why: Other planets have moons, air and orbits. Only the Earth has liquid water on its surface, and it is the only world where we know living beings exist.

quiz.p: Which of these bodies goes round a planet?
quiz.why: The Moon goes round the Earth. Ceres, Eris and Vesta all go round the Sun.

quiz.p: Which of these is most likely to be lumpy?
quiz.why: A small body has weak gravity, so it cannot pull its bumps down. Phobos is shaped like a potato. The other three are round.

quiz.p: Titan, a moon of Saturn, is 5,150 km wide. Mercury is 4,879 km wide. What can you say?
opts: A moon can be wider than a planet
quiz.why: Titan is wider than Mercury, but it goes round Saturn, so it is a moon. Choosing 'Titan is a planet' uses width as the test.

quiz.p: Where is the balance point of the Earth and the Moon?
opts: Inside the Earth, about 4,700 km from its centre
Outside the Earth, near the Moon
quiz.why: The Earth has 81 times the Moon's mass. 384,400 ÷ 82 is about 4,700 km. The Earth's radius is 6,371 km, so the point is inside it.

quiz.p: A heavy ball and a light ball turn on a thread tied at their balance point. Which ball makes the smaller circle?
opts: Neither, because the heavy ball stays still
quiz.why: The heavy ball is nearer the balance point, so its circle is smaller. It still goes round, as it did in The Two-Ball Balance.

quiz.p: With the Earth as a marble, the Sun is a ball as tall as a grown-up. About how far apart are they?
quiz.why: The Sun is about 11,700 Earth-widths away. A marble 1.6 cm wide gives about 187 metres.

quiz.p: A ball is twice as wide as another, made of the same dough. How much more dough does it hold?
quiz.why: It is twice as wide, as tall and as deep. 2 x 2 x 2 = 8.

quiz.p: How does the Sun's mass compare with the mass of all the planets together?
quiz.why: The Sun has about 333,000 Earth masses. All the planets together have about 450. So the Sun has more than 700 times as much.

quiz.p: Pluto goes round the Sun and is round. Which test does it fail?
opts: It does not go round the Sun
It has not cleared its path
quiz.why: Pluto shares its path with thousands of icy bodies. That is why it is a dwarf planet.

quiz.p: Voyager 1 left the Sun's bubble of gas in 2012. Has it left the solar system?
opts: It depends on how the edge is measured
No, it is still between Mars and Jupiter
Nobody can tell where it is
quiz.why: By the Sun's wind, it has left. By the Sun's gravity, it is still deep inside. There is no single agreed edge.

quiz.p: On a clear night in India, the stars seem to circle round one point in the north sky. Why does the Pole Star hardly seem to move?
opts: It sits almost exactly over the Earth's north pole, the point the spin turns round
It is a planet that stands still in the sky
It is the nearest star to the Earth
The Earth stops spinning for the Pole Star
quiz.why: The Earth spins on its axis, and the axis points almost at the Pole Star. So the sky seems to turn round that star. It is not a planet. It is a star far outside the solar system. The Earth never stops spinning, and the Pole Star is not the nearest star.

videos.why: To see how astronomers find planets round other stars. It goes well with The Hidden Ball.

applications: Astronomers find planets round other stars by the small wobble that each planet causes in her star. Thousands of planets have been found this way and by other methods.
Television, phone and weather satellites sit about 36,000 km above the Earth. At that height they go round once a day. So a rooftop dish can point at one spot in the sky for ever.
India's Aditya-L1 spacecraft stays about 1.5 million km from the Earth, in a spot between the Earth and the Sun. The pulls of the Earth and the Sun are balanced there.
Map makers, architects and model engineers all use one scale for every length in a model. A model with two scales would mislead people.
A cook who needs a pot that holds 8 times as much rice buys a pot of the same shape that is only twice as wide. The same cube rule tells engineers how much a tank holds.
Astronomers use the three tests of 2006 to sort each new round, icy world found beyond Neptune. This tells them how it fits into the solar system.
The Moon's pull on the Earth lifts the tides. The Earth and the Moon pull on each other, and that is why both go round the balance point they share.

spotted.art: A bright dot above the rooftops of a city just after sunset, with a few small stars higher in the sky.

spotted.text: A TV dish on a roof. It always points at the same spot in the sky, where a satellite sits 36,000 km up.
spotted.art: A white TV dish on a flat roof, pointing to a small satellite drawn in the sky.

spotted.text: A bright dot that moves smoothly across the sky in a few minutes, with no blinking light. It may be the International Space Station.
spotted.art: A long thin trail of light crossing a dark evening sky above a row of coconut trees.

spotted.text: A cloud picture on the weather forecast on television. It was taken by a weather satellite going round the Earth.

spotted.text: A planet next to the crescent Moon, on an evening when the two come close. A phone sky app tells you which planet it is.
spotted.art: A thin crescent Moon with a bright dot close beside it over a quiet street.

spotted.text: The Aryabhata satellite on the back of an old 2-rupee note, in a family collection or a museum.

open_questions.q: Is there a ninth planet far beyond Neptune?
open_questions.why_open: Several icy bodies have paths that lean the same way, which an unseen planet could explain. Nobody has found one, and some astronomers think the pattern is chance.

open_questions.q: How exactly did the Moon form?
open_questions.why_open: The leading idea is a crash with a world the size of Mars. But Moon rock is very like Earth rock, which a simple crash does not explain, so the details are still argued over.

open_questions.q: How did Triton, Neptune's big moon, come to go round Neptune backwards, against the way Neptune spins?
open_questions.why_open: Some scientists think Neptune caught Triton from the Kuiper belt. Nobody has shown how a world that big could be caught and settle into a round path.

open_questions.q: What is in the Oort cloud, and how far does it reach?
open_questions.why_open: Nobody has seen it. Its size and its number of icy bodies are worked out from the paths of comets, so they could be wrong.

open_questions.q: Why do other planetary systems often have planets between the sizes of the Earth and Neptune, when ours has none?
open_questions.why_open: Many systems found so far have such planets close to their star. Astronomers do not yet know whether ours is unusual, or whether telescopes find those planets more easily.

ask_kids: Which is bigger, the planet Mercury or Ganymede, the moon of Jupiter? Which is called a planet?
If the Earth is a marble, how far away would the Sun be? How long would it take you to walk there?
Who in our family would be nearer the balance point on a see-saw, the heavier person or the lighter one?
How many small boxes would fit in a box twice as wide as the small box? Look at the cupboard and test it.
Which things around us were made by people and go round the Earth? Which things go round it without help?
Pluto was a planet when your grandparents were at school. What other things have changed their names or their groups since then?
Why do you think the pictures of the planets in a book put them so close together?
If we sent a message to a spacecraft past Neptune, would it be answered before dinner? Why?

jokes.j: How does the solar system keep its trousers up?
How do you throw a party in space?
What is a planet's favourite kind of music?
Why did the dwarf planet fail its test?
jokes.a: It could not clear its path.
Everyone called it a mere moon, though it was wider than Mercury.

jokes.j: Why did the child bring a ruler to the planetarium?
jokes.a: To check that the show was drawn to scale.

jokes.j: Why did the Sun not need a map?
jokes.a: Everyone else went round it, so it knew where everyone was.

jokes.j: What did the heavy ball say to the light ball on the pencil?
jokes.a: I will meet you near me.

jokes.j: What did Pluto say after the vote of 2006?
jokes.a: Call me what you like. I am still going round the Sun.

maths.problem: In Marble Earth, Peppercorn Moon, 1 cm stands for 8,000 km. Mars is 6,779 km wide. How wide is a model Mars?
maths.explain: 6,779 divided by 8,000 is about 0.85. So a model Mars is a little over half as wide as the 1.6 cm marble Earth.
maths.context: In Marble Earth, Peppercorn Moon, a marble stands for the Earth on the scale of 1 cm for 8,000 km. You can use the same scale for other worlds.
maths.why_maths: A scale turns every real size into a model size by one division, so every world in the model is in proportion.

maths.problem: In the made-up results of The Two-Ball Balance, 4 pieces against 1 gave parts of 14.1 cm and 3.9 cm. How many times as long is the long part? Is that close to 4?
maths.explain: 14.1 divided by 3.9 is about 3.6. The rule says 4. The pencil itself has weight too. Its weight is spread along its whole length, so it moves the balance point a little towards the middle of the pencil.
maths.context: In The Two-Ball Balance, you divide the long part of the pencil by the short part for each pair. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: Dividing one part by the other shows how well the results match the rule, and a small difference points to a reason.

maths.problem: In Twice as Wide, a dough ball is 12 cm wide. A small ball is 2 cm wide. How many small balls would fill it?
maths.explain: 12 divided by 2 is 6, so the big ball is 6 times as wide. 6 x 6 x 6 = 216.
maths.context: In Twice as Wide, balls 2 times and 3 times as wide held 8 and 27 small balls. Here is a bigger ball.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying a number by itself three times is called cubing it. It turns how many times as wide into how many times as much.

maths.problem: In A Thousand Grains of Rice, Jupiter has 1 grain of the 1,000. What percentage of the solar system's mass is that?
maths.explain: 1 divided by 1,000 is 0.001. As a percentage, that is 0.1 percent. So 99.9 percent of the mass is not Jupiter.
maths.context: In A Thousand Grains of Rice, 1,000 grains stand for the mass of the whole solar system. Jupiter has about one grain.
maths.why_maths: A percentage makes a tiny share easy to compare. Jupiter is the heaviest planet, and still holds only a tenth of one percent.

maths.problem: A book's picture shows the Earth 3 mm wide and the Sun 30 mm from it. The true distance is 11,700 Earth-widths. How many times too small is the drawn distance?
maths.explain: The true distance on the same scale is 3 x 11,700 = 35,100 mm. 35,100 divided by 30 is 1,170. So the picture has squeezed the gap 1,170 times.
maths.context: In Fix the Picture, you measured the Earth and the Sun's distance in a book's picture. These are made-up measurements.
maths.why_maths: Big numbers turn a vague feeling that a picture is off into an exact amount that you can say aloud.

maths.problem: On the strip in An Honest Solar System, 1 astronomical unit is 3.5 cm. Saturn is 9.5 astronomical units from the Sun. How far along the strip is Saturn?
maths.explain: 9.5 x 3.5 = 33.25. So Saturn's dot goes about 33 cm from the Sun.
maths.context: In An Honest Solar System, you mark each planet on a long strip of paper, using one scale for the distances.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying each distance by the same number keeps every planet in the right place compared with the others.

maths.problem: In The Hidden Ball, the visible ball has 3 pieces. The pencil is 20 cm long. The visible ball swings 10 cm wide. How many pieces are hidden?
maths.explain: The visible ball swings in a circle 10 cm wide, so it is 5 cm from the thread. The pencil is 20 cm long, so the hidden ball is 20 - 5 = 15 cm from the thread. 15 is 3 times 5, so the visible ball is 3 times as heavy as the hidden ball. The visible ball has 3 pieces, so the hidden ball has 3 divided by 3, which is 1 piece.
maths.context: In The Hidden Ball, you find the weight of a hidden ball from how far the visible ball swings. These are made-up numbers.
maths.why_maths: The missing number comes from the balance rule: weights are in the opposite ratio to the distances.

warmup.q: Where is the balance point of the Earth and the Moon?
warmup.a: Inside the Earth, about 4,700 km from its centre.

quiz: A moon can be wider than a planet.
Ganymede and Titan are both wider than Mercury.
Pluto stopped being a planet because it shrank.
Pluto did not change. It has not cleared its path, so it fails the third test.
The Earth and the Moon both go round a point inside the Earth.
The point is about 4,700 km from the Earth's centre.
A ball twice as wide holds four times as much.
It holds 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 times as much.
The Sun holds more than 99 percent of the solar system's mass.
All the planets together are less than 2 parts in 1,000.
With the Earth as a marble, the Moon is a peppercorn about 48 cm away.
The Moon is about 30 Earth-widths away.
Book pictures of the solar system show the true distances.
They squeeze the distances far more than the sizes, so everything fits on a page.
Ganymede is the biggest moon in the solar system.
It is 5,268 km wide, wider than Mercury.
Neptune is about 30 times as far from the Sun as the Earth.
It is 30 astronomical units out.
The solar system has one edge that everyone agrees on.
The edge depends on what you measure: the planets, the Sun's wind or the Sun's gravity.
odd: Ceres, Pluto and Eris are dwarf planets that go round the Sun. Ganymede is a moon of Jupiter.
The Moon, Titan and Phobos are moons. Mars is a planet.
Mercury, Venus and Mars are rocky planets. Jupiter is a giant of gas.
Three of these were made by people. Halley's Comet is a natural lump of ice and dust.
The Sun, Sirius and Proxima Centauri are stars. Jupiter is a planet and makes no light of its own.
